AEP25: los Estados Partes deben traducir su apoyo a la justicia internacional en acciones concretas
articles.description: 2026/11/24 AEP25: los Estados Partes deben traducir su apoyo a la justicia internacional en acciones concretas Introductory text: Este mes, la 25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma de la CPI se celebrará en La Haya, del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026, en un contexto de crecientes ataques contra la independencia de la Corte Penal Internacional, sus operaciones y las personas y organizaciones que hacen posible su labor. De cara al período de sesiones, la Coalición por la Corte Penal Internacional (CCPI) publica su documento de referencia para la AEP25
paragraphs: Las sanciones contra la institución amenazan servicios esenciales, las órdenes de detención siguen sin ejecutarse y las organizaciones de la sociedad civil sufren represalias por promover la rendición de cuentas. Para las víctimas y las personas supervivientes, estos ataques ponen en peligro la posibilidad misma de obtener justicia. Mientras se preparan para reunirse en su período de sesiones anual, los Estados Partes deben traducir sus compromisos con el Estatuto de Roma en protección, recursos y cooperación concretos.

Al mismo tiempo, la Corte y las organizaciones de la sociedad civil prosiguen su labor con determinación. Está previsto que comiencen dos juicios en las situaciones de Libia y Filipinas, que permitirán avanzar hacia la justicia que miles de víctimas llevan tanto tiempo esperando.
En la AEP25, los Estados Partes deben demostrar que su compromiso con el Estatuto de Roma se corresponde con las decisiones, los recursos y las medidas prácticas necesarios para defenderlo.

Este año ha puesto de manifiesto tanto las posibilidades de la justicia internacional como la fragilidad de las condiciones de las que depende. Los procedimientos relativos a las situaciones en Filipinas y Libia han abierto oportunidades largamente esperadas para que se escuchen las voces de las víctimas. La sociedad civil ha seguido documentando crímenes, apoyando a las personas supervivientes y exigiendo rendición de cuentas. Sin embargo, estos esfuerzos se desarrollan en un contexto de sanciones, injerencias políticas, incumplimiento de las órdenes de detención y presiones financieras que amenazan la capacidad de la Corte para hacer justicia.

La designación de la CPI como institución sujeta a sanciones por parte de Estados Unidos el 9 de octubre de 2026 supuso una grave escalada de los ataques que ya afectaban a funcionarios de la Corte y organizaciones de la sociedad civil. Las consecuencias van más allá de quienes son objeto directo de las sanciones: las restricciones a los servicios bancarios, tecnológicos y otros servicios esenciales obstaculizan la labor de rendición de cuentas, mientras que la amenaza de nuevas medidas desalienta la cooperación y aísla a quienes buscan justicia. La presión sobre los Estados Partes para que reconsideren su adhesión al Estatuto de Roma amenaza, además, el alcance del sistema y su capacidad para cumplir sus compromisos sin coacción externa.

Estos ataques coinciden con un incumplimiento persistente de las obligaciones de cooperación con la Corte. La ejecución de las órdenes de detención depende de la actuación de los Estados, pero las consideraciones políticas siguen obstaculizándola. Las remisiones a la Asamblea relativas a Italia y Tayikistán le confieren una responsabilidad particular: garantizar un seguimiento político y diplomático sostenido de las constataciones judiciales de falta de cooperación. Para las víctimas y los testigos, la falta de detención y entrega de las personas sospechosas puede prolongar la inseguridad, agravar el temor a las represalias y socavar la confianza en que su colaboración con la Corte conducirá a la rendición de cuentas.
articles.lede: Las sanciones contra la institución amenazan servicios esenciales, las órdenes de detención siguen sin ejecutarse y las organizaciones de la sociedad civil sufren represalias por promover la rendición de cuentas.

articles.title: ASP25: States Parties must turn support for international justice into concrete action
articles.description: 2026/11/24 ASP25: States Parties must turn support for international justice into concrete action Introductory text: This month, the 25th session of the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute of the ICC will take place in the Hague from 30 November and 7 December 2026 amid escalating attacks on the International Criminal Court’s independence, its operations and the people and organisations making its work possible. Ahead of the session, the Coalition for the International Criminal Court (CICC) publishes its ASP25 background document. Drawing on year-round civil society monitoring, expe
paragraphs: Institutional sanctions threaten essential services, arrest warrants remain unenforced, and civil society organisations face retaliation for pursuing accountability. For victims and survivors, these attacks threaten the prospect of justice itself. As States Parties prepare to gather for their annual session, they must turn their commitments to the Rome Statute into concrete protection, resources and cooperation.

At the same time, the Court and civil society organisations continue their work undeterred. Two trials are set to open in the Libya and Philippines situation, bringing long awaited justice to thousands of victims.
At ASP25, States Parties must demonstrate that their commitment to the Rome Statute is matched by the decisions, resources and practical measures needed to uphold it.

This year has demonstrated both the possibilities of international justice and the fragility of the conditions on which it depends. Proceedings in the Situations in the Philippines and Libya situations have brought long-awaited opportunities for victims’ voices to be heard. Civil society has continued documenting crimes, supporting survivors, and pressing for accountability. Yet these efforts take place amid sanctions, political interference, failures to execute arrest warrants, and financial pressures that threaten the Court’s ability to deliver justice.

The United States’ designation of the ICC as an institution on 9 October 2026 marked a major escalation in attacks already targeting Court officials and civil society organisations. The consequences extend beyond those directly sanctioned: restrictions on banking, technology and other essential services disrupt accountability work, while the threat of further measures discourages cooperation and isolates those seeking justice. Pressure on States Parties to reconsider their Rome Statute membership further threatens the system’s reach and their ability to uphold their commitments free from external coercion.

These attacks coincide with persistent failures to cooperate with the Court. Arrest warrants depend on States taking action, yet political considerations continue to obstruct their execution. The referrals concerning Italy and Tajikistan place a particular responsibility on the Assembly to ensure that judicial findings of non-cooperation receive sustained political and diplomatic follow-up. For victims and witnesses, failures to arrest and surrender suspects can prolong insecurity, deepen fears of reprisals and undermine confidence that engagement with the Court will lead to accountability.

At the same time, the Court must maintain investigations, conduct fair proceedings, protect witnesses and give practical effect to victims’ rights under growing financial and operational pressure. Its proposed 2027 budget must be considered against both its judicial workload and the additional demands of protecting staff, strengthening cybersecurity and maintaining essential services. Outreach, interpretation, legal representation and field engagement are equally necessary: proceedings cannot deliver meaningful justice if affected communities cannot understand, access or participate in them.
articles.lede: Institutional sanctions threaten essential services, arrest warrants remain unenforced, and civil society organisations face retaliation for pursuing accountability.

articles.title: Europe’s Courts Become Last Resort for Protecting Those Who Help Migrants
articles.description: For most volunteers in the European Union prosecuted for providing humanitarian aid to migrants, courts have proved the strongest safeguard.
paragraphs: On Nov. 25, a regional court in Latvia will hear the appeal of Ieva Raubiško, a human rights defender convicted last year for helping five Syrian asylum seekers stranded at the country’s border with Belarus. Her case is one of dozens across Europe. The Brussels-based nonprofit Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants recorded at least 110 people facing judicial proceedings in the European Union in 2025 for helping migrants and asylum seekers, most of them in Greece and Poland.

Raubiško was prosecuted after she had secured an “ interim measure” ruling from the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) in Strasbourg requiring Latvia not to deport the group of migrants, who border guards had already pushed back into Belarus repeatedly, and to provide them with food, water, clothing, adequate medical assistance, and temporary housing. When Raubiško and another activist went to the border to check whether the authorities were complying, border guards detained them both.

Governments across Europe have tightened border controls and some have restricted access to asylum. Authorities have also used anti-smuggling laws to penalize people who help migrants and asylum seekers, including for handing out food and water. Such prosecutions have continued even as irregular crossings at the EU’s external borders fell to nearly 178,000 in 2025, less than half the 2023 total. The cases rarely hold up; of the 41 people whose proceedings for helping migrants ended in 2025, 38 were acquitted or had their charges dropped. For most volunteers prosecuted over humanitarian aid, the courts have proved the strongest safeguard. Latvia’s appeal court now has the chance to do the same for Raubiško.

The issue of migration in Latvia, as in Poland, returned to the fore in 2021, when Belarus, a close ally of Russia, began luring people from countries including Iraq and Afghanistan and to a lesser extent from Syria, Congo-Brazzaville, and Russia to its capital Minsk with promises of passage into the EU. Belarusian authorities arranged transport for the migrants to its borders with Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia. Most of the people crossing are fleeing conflict and persecution in the Middle East and Africa, and Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko appears to be using them in a gambit to destabilize the EU with an issue that has long created significant political ruptures across the Union.

Latvian authorities say that, between Aug. 10, 2021, through June 27, 2026, they prevented more than 47,000 attempted crossings from Belarus into their country of more than 1.8 million people. In practice, many people are pushed back into Belarus, often more than once. Under a state of emergency in effect from August 2021 to August 2023, Latvian border guards could force people back into Belarus, and Amnesty International documented beatings, secret detention in guarded forest tents, and coerced “voluntary” returns. A 2023 law now allows border guards to “prevent” crossings, which in practice can amount to unlawful summary returns. Like Poland and Lithuania, Latvia has fenced its border with Belarus, completing a barrier along nearly 145 kilometers (90 miles) of it in 2024 and adding surveillance technology. This summer, Latvian border guards found two tunnels dug under the border.
articles.lede: For most volunteers in the European Union prosecuted for providing humanitarian aid to migrants, courts have proved the strongest safeguard.

articles.title: With Genocide Ruling, Justice Finally Descends Upon Myanmar and the Rohingya
Could This Be the End of Bivens?
articles.description: It’s going to be up to Congress to restore the federal government’s accountability for unconstitutional misconduct by federal officials.
paragraphs: Oral argument last week in Nielsen v. Watanabe, the Supreme Court’s most recent prisoner civil rights case, suggests that the Court’s war on government accountability is continuing apace. The Court appears poised to foreclose–or at least drastically restrict–constitutional damage actions by federal prisoners, raising a question that would have seemed far-fetched a decade ago: Could this be the end of Bivens?

The case was brought by a federal prisoner, Kekai Watanabe, seeking damages for an alleged violation of the Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause. In his lawsuit, Watanabe alleges that after a July 2021 attack by other prisoners broke his tailbone leaving him in excruciating pain, a Federal Bureau of Prisons staff nurse, Francis Nielsen, was deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs, telling him to “stop being a cry baby” and offering him only over-the-counter pain relief rather than treatment. The Supreme Court granted certiorari review to decide whether Watanabe can pursue damages under Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971).

Watanabe’s path should have been an easy one. After all, in Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S. 14 (1980), the Court recognized a damages remedy available in an Eighth Amendment claim of deliberate indifference to medical needs where federal prison officials allegedly left a prisoner without competent care for hours during an asthma attack, gave him drugs that made the attack worse, tried to use a respirator they knew was broken, and delayed his transfer to an outside hospital; he died. True, the Supreme Court has been cutting back on Bivens for decades, especially sharply since 2017. But the Court has framed its approach as declining to “apply[] Bivens in a new context.”

Watanabe makes a persuasive case that he is not asking the Court to extend Bivens at all. As his brief, filed by lawyers from the prisoners’ advocacy organization Rights Behind Bars and Weil Gotshal, explains, “Watanabe asserts the same kind of violation of the same constitutional right by the same type of defendant in the same institutional setting pursuant to the same substantive standards as the plaintiff in Carlson. This is precisely the kind of claim this Court has long understood Carlson to encompass.”

But Watanabe has the better of an additional argument, too: two statutes show that Congress was content to allow Carlson to remain the rule. The 1988 Westfall Act made the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) the “exclusive” remedy for torts by government employees, eliminating state common law remedies prisoners historically might have pursued against federal officers. But the Westfall Act expressly stated that it did not exclude civil actions against a federal employee “brought for a violation of the Constitution.” 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b)(2)(A). And the 1996 Prison Litigation Reform Act (PLRA)—though it put a large number of obstacles in the way of prisoner lawsuits—filing fees, exhaustion requirements, limitations on damages, and more—did not abrogate Carlson’s damages remedy.
articles.lede: It’s going to be up to Congress to restore the federal government’s accountability for unconstitutional misconduct by federal officials.

articles.title: On a Matter or Involving It? What the BBNJ COP Can Ask ITLOS about Other Bodies
cats: International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea
articles.description: The first meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP) to the BBNJ Agreement opens in New York on 11 January 2027. Among the rules of procedure recommended by the Preparatory Commission is draft …
paragraphs: The first meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP) to the BBNJ Agreement opens in New York on 11 January 2027. Among the rules of procedure recommended by the Preparatory Commission is draft rule 48, which would require the COP, once it decides to ask the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) for an advisory opinion on a proposal, to defer its decision on that proposal until the opinion arrives. The rule operationalises Article 47(7) of the Agreement, which allows the COP to request an opinion on a legal question concerning the conformity with the Agreement of a proposal before it.

Article 47(7) has mostly been discussed as part of the debate on the full Tribunal’s advisory jurisdiction, which some regard as settled and which China, in the COSIS proceedings, accepted only for COP requests ‘and nothing else’. The requesting power itself is ‘narrowly defined’, and its most consequential limit excludes requests ‘on a matter within the competences of other global, regional, subregional or sectoral bodies’. Since area-based management tools (ABMTs), the likeliest subject of a request, will often overlap with fisheries bodies, the IMO or the International Seabed Authority (ISA), that limit will largely decide whether the mechanism can be used.

This post argues that Article 47(7) separates two things that are easily run together: a question whose answer requires the Tribunal to consider a matter, and a request on that matter. For sovereignty disputes and the status of areas, the provision excludes the first. For other bodies, it excludes only the second. What counts is the object of the determination the Tribunal is asked to make.

Article 5(2) requires the Agreement to be interpreted and applied in a manner that does not undermine relevant bodies, and Article 22(2) requires decisions on ABMTs to respect their competences. Whether a proposal meets those obligations is likely to be the central legal question in any contested ABMT. If the exclusion bites whenever another body’s competence is engaged, the COP could seek advice on everything except that question. Kuc accordingly describes the limitation as ‘very far-reaching and problematic’, and Mossop has asked whether it might prevent the Tribunal from considering whether a proposal undermines another body.

The most developed analysis, by Schatz, Bertram and Ipsen, draws on jurisdictional practice under UNCLOS to outline an interpretation under which the Tribunal may assess whether a proposal respects another body’s competence under Article 22(2), while determinations on the substance of matters within that competence remain excluded. This post asks what the text of Article 47(7) itself contributes to separating permissible analysis from excluded determinations, a question that has received less attention.

Article 47(7) excludes two kinds of request in one sentence, using two formulas. Requests are excluded ‘on a matter within the competences’ of other bodies, and ‘on a matter that necessarily involves the concurrent consideration’ of a dispute over land territory or of the legal status of an area as within national jurisdiction. The second formula, which appears to draw on Article 298(1)(a) UNCLOS, belongs to the law of incidental jurisdiction. It looks at the route to an answer and catches any question that cannot be answered without deciding such a dispute, however the question is framed. It addresses a familiar problem, the repackaging of sovereignty disputes as questions of treaty interpretation (see the recent assessment report of the China Institute for Marine Affairs, June 2026, paras 24 and 39). The first formula contains no such extension, and it looks at what the request is about.
articles.lede: The first meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP) to the BBNJ Agreement opens in New York on 11 January 2027.

articles.title: Pakistan: Human rights organisations call for release of political prisoner Idris Khattak
articles.description: Idris Khattak has been detained since 13 November 2019, because of his human rights work. On the seven-year anniversary of Idris Khattak’s (…)
paragraphs: Idris Khattak has been detained since 13 November 2019, because of his human rights work. On the seven-year anniversary of Idris Khattak’s detention in Pakistan, the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership between the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), along with the undersigned organisations, calls for his immediate and unconditional release.

Idris Khattak is a well-known Pashtun human rights defender who spent decades documenting human rights abuses, including enforced disappearances, in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province and the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas. On 13 November 2019, he was abducted and disappeared. For the next seven months, his family did not know whether he was alive or dead.

In June 2020, Pakistani authorities finally admitted that Khattak was in the custody of the country’s military intelligence service. In late 2021, he was convicted by a military court of violating the notorious Official Secrets Act, a law that UN experts have described as “yet another means of silencing dissent from human rights defenders.” He was sentenced to 14 years in prison. His trial was marked by egregious due process violations—it was held in secret, he was denied access to counsel, a forced confession was introduced as evidence, the prosecution relied on secret evidence that was never shown to the defense, and he was not allowed to present key defense witnesses.

Khattak’s detention has been widely condemned. UN special procedure mandate holders described his conviction as an “attack against the human rights community in Pakistan” and noted that his detention is “emblematic of how the military justice system is being instrumentalized to repress critical voices and rights activists.” The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention concluded that “Khattak was detained as a result of his work as a human rights defender” and called for his immediate release. His case has been raised by members of the US Congress and the European Parliament.

We are particularly concerned that Khattak has been denied adequate medical care, including for his diabetes, and as a result, his health has deteriorated significantly. In February 2026, Dr. Michele Heisler, a Harvard-trained physician and diabetes expert, provided an independent medical evaluation of Khattak’s health status. After reviewing his medical records, she concluded that “ considering the current conditions of Mr. Khattak’s detention, including his limited access to medication and medical care, his health—and his life—is at serious risk.” In April 2026, UN experts similarly expressed “grave concerns about the deteriorating and life-threatening health risks” he faces in prison, noting that he is “already showing serious symptoms of uncontrolled diabetes.” Since then, Khattak’s health has deteriorated further, yet Pakistani authorities continue to deny him an independent medical exam and appropriate medication and treatment.

articles.title: Pakistani Prisoners Face Poor Access to Health Care
articles.description: Authorities should ensure all prisoners, regardless of political affiliation or status, receive timely and adequate medical care, with continuity of treatment.
paragraphs: When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.

Human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care. Many inmates who fall ill in custody fail to receive prompt or decent care at all.

After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.

Colonial-era laws have long-enabled Pakistani officials and powerful people to interfere in prison operations, sometimes making use of poor conditions to harass jailed political opponents. In a November 16 letter released by his lawyer, former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed for urgent medical care for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, citing his high blood pressure and her need for eye surgery. Khan’s appeal echoes complaints about medical care in custody from former President Asif Ali Zardari and former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. All have alleged that prison services denied access to medical care as a form of punishment.

Federal and provincial governments in Pakistan should bring health care in jails and prisons in line with international standards, notably the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Mandela Rules ), which require that prisoners receive necessary free medical care to the same standard available in the community, with prompt attention in emergencies. In October, Justice Project Pakistan called for common standards across provinces so prisoners can see medical specialists when needed and continue treatment after release.

Pakistan’s federal and provincial governments should provide prescribed medicines free of charge and require prisons to record how long patients wait for care. When care requires an urgent hospital transfer, prison authorities should promptly facilitate transport. Authorities should ensure all prisoners, regardless of political affiliation or status, receive timely and adequate medical care, with continuity of treatment.
articles.lede: Authorities should ensure all prisoners, regardless of political affiliation or status, receive timely and adequate medical care, with continuity of treatment.

articles.title: Éthiopie: Amnesty réclame une enquête sur de possibles crimes de guerre de l'armée fédérale au Tigré
articles.description: Évoquant « des attaques aveugles », Amnesty International a réclamé, mardi 24 novembre 2026, une enquête sur de possibles crimes de guerre de l'armée fédérale éthiopienne et de ses alliés au Tigré après…
paragraphs: Évoquant « des attaques aveugles », Amnesty International a réclamé, mardi 24 novembre 2026, une enquête sur de possibles crimes de guerre de l'armée fédérale éthiopienne et de ses alliés au Tigré après la mort, fin septembre, de 14 civils dans des tirs d'artillerie sur une ville de la région. Les forces du TPLF ont de leur côté « mis des civils en danger en établissant des bases militaires dans des zones résidentielles peuplées », a ajouté l'ONG.

Dans un rapport publié mardi 24 novembre, Amnesty International réclame une enquête sur de possibles crimes de guerre commis par l’armée fédérale éthiopienne à Alamata, dans le sud du Tigré, entre le 26 et le 28 septembre.

D’après l’ONG, 14 personnes seraient mortes après des tirs d’artillerie, dont trois enfants. Amnesty accuse aussi le Front de libération du peuple du Tigré (TPLF) d’avoir mis en danger les civils, en établissant des bases militaires dans des zones résidentielles peuplées.

L'un des quartiers les plus durement touchés par les bombardements est celui dit « des copropriétés », une zone résidentielle très peuplée, composée de maisons et de deux immeubles de plusieurs étages. Le 27 septembre, à l’aube, un tir d’artillerie a touché cinq habitations, tuant sept personnes sur le coup.

Parmi les victimes figurent Meron Sewasew, une jeune femme de 26 ans et son fils de huit ans, Markon Girmahiwot. « Ils étaient restés dans la maison pour être à l’abri de la guerre, a déclaré le mari de la victime. C’était mon amour de lycée. Notre histoire s’est terminée trop tôt ».
Cette même attaque a tué quatre membres d'une famille vivant juste à côté, dont deux enfants de 14 et 3 ans.

Le même jour, Selam était à Alamata quand des tirs se sont abattus sur le marché. « J’ai vu de mes propres yeux des morts et des blessés. Certains avaient la moitié du visage arraché », a-t-elle raconté à RFI. « C’était le chaos partout. »
Contacté par Amnesty, le TPLF a « catégoriquement rejeté » les allégations portées contre lui. L’armée fédérale, elle, n’a pas répondu.
À lire aussi Éthiopie: quatre ans après l’accord de paix de Pretoria, que sont devenus les déplacés tigréens?

Le Tigré, région du nord de l'Éthiopie, avait déjà connu des crimes de guerre, selon les ONG de défense des droits humains, lors du conflit extrêmement sanglant qui s'y est déroulé de 2020 à 2022. Celui-ci, l'un des plus meurtriers de ces dernières années dans le monde, avait fait au moins 600 000 morts, selon une estimation de l'Union africaine jugée basse par de nombreux experts.
articles.lede: Évoquant « des attaques aveugles », Amnesty International a réclamé, mardi 24 novembre 2026, une enquête sur de possibles crimes de guerre de l'armée fédérale éthiopienne et de ses alliés au Tigré après la mort, fin…

articles.title: Azerbaijan: Civil society organisations call on OSCE participating States to block an Azerbaijani bid for the Chairpersonship-in-Office
articles.description: In recent discussions at the OSCE Permanent Council, including on 19 November 2026, participating States discussed the possibility of an (…)
paragraphs: In recent discussions at the OSCE Permanent Council, including on 19 November 2026, participating States discussed the possibility of an Azerbaijani OSCE Chairpersonship-in-Office (CiO) in 2027. The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership between the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), together with other civil society organisations, expresses its firm opposition to a potential Azerbaijani CiO and calls on participating States to block any such decision.

We, the undersigned civil society organisations, are writing to express our firm opposition to a potential Azerbaijani OSCE Chairpersonship-in-Office (CiO) and call on participating States to block any such decision. The Azerbaijani government is not a reliable security, environmental, or human rights partner and is unfit to chair the organisation.

In recent discussions at the Permanent Council, including on 19 November 2026, participating States discussed the possibility of an Azerbaijani CiO 2027. This is deeply troubling, especially given the understandable focus of many participating States on putting the organisation on more stable footing. But leaving the organisation in the hands of an authoritarian government would seriously question the legitimacy and credibility of a body tasked with promoting a comprehensive security approach which includes human rights among its core pillars.

As OSCE participating States reassess security priorities in the face of growing authoritarianism, geopolitical instability, and hybrid threats, they must recognise that authoritarian States, including Azerbaijan, increasingly threaten European security through disinformation, corruption, political interference, transnational repression, and efforts to undermine democratic institutions. A strong, independent, and resilient civil society is an essential component of a comprehensive security architecture. Yet, Azerbaijan has, since 2013, implemented a massive crackdown on independent Azerbaijani civil society, including NGOs, media outlets, and human rights defenders, including journalists and human rights lawyers. The crackdown has intensified since the end of 2023, with further restrictions to the civic space and public participation in Azerbaijan. There are over 300 political prisoners behind bars, as documented by Azerbaijani human rights groups, with dozens of civic actors imprisoned in retaliation for their legitimate human rights and media work, including abroad.

In recent years, the European Court of Human Rights, the European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission) and the UN Committee against Torture have found that Azerbaijan’s legislation is not in line with international standards regarding the regulation of civil society and media organisations. In October, the European Parliament adopted by a wide margin a resolution condemning the misuse by Azerbaijani authorities of national security laws to silence NGOs and the media, and transnational repression against dissenting and opposition voices. The resolution also criticised the Azerbaijani authorities for the on-going politically motivated incarceration of human rights defenders, including Anar Mammadli, who was detained in 2024 following his advocacy at the OSCE, among other multilateral institutions. A resolution adopted by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) in June 2026, recognised the systemic silencing of dissent in Azerbaijan, including the dismantling of independent media, the rise in reported political prisoners, the misuse of criminal law, and the role of restrictive NGO and media legislation in suppressing civic space. At the European Court for Human Rights, Azerbaijan remains one of the States with the highest percentage of non-implementation of judgements, demonstrating an unwillingness to meet its commitments under the European Convention on Human Rights.

articles.title: Not Proven is Not Peace: The Said Judgment and Classifying Conflict Beyond Reasonable Doubt
General Intent in Gambia v. Myanmar
articles.description: Analysis of the International Court of Justice's judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar on genocide.
paragraphs: Genocide is a “dual intent” crime. Listed acts must be committed with both general intent and the specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part. In simple terms, general intent involves the perpetrator’s mental state with respect to their own conduct and its direct consequences for individual victims, while specific intent involves the perpetrator’s mental state with respect to the broader consequences of their conduct for the victim group as such. Both are required. The Gambia had to show that Myanmar’s security forces killed, injured, and prevented births among individual victims with general intent, and that Myanmar specifically intended to thereby destroy a substantial part of the victims’ group. While specific intent involves the purpose or aim to bring about a result, the Court clarified that general intent is a broader concept.

In Gambia v. Myanmar, the Court returned to the same passage of the ILC Commentary, which continues: “[t]he prohibited acts enumerated in subparagraphs (a) to (e) are by their very nature conscious, intentional or volitional acts which an individual could not usually commit without knowing that certain consequences were likely to result” (emphasis added).

the words “killing” and “meurtre” appear in the English and French versions respectively of subparagraph (a) of Article II of the Convention. For the Court, these words have the same meaning, and refer to the act of intentionally killing members of the group (I.C.J. Reports 2007 (I), p. 121, para. 186 and Blagojević and Jokić, IT‑02‑60‑T, Trial Chamber, Judgment of 17 January 2005, para. 642).

In Gambia v. Myanmar, the Court picked up where it left off, citing the same ICTY Trial Chamber judgment in Blagojević and Jokić as well as ICTY Trial Chamber judgments in Karadžić and Krstić and the ECCC Trial Chamber judgment in Case 002/02 (Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan). The Court observed

that the expression “intentional killing” has been given the same meaning as “murder” within the definition of crimes against humanity in the jurisprudence of international criminal tribunals. In the Court’s view, a killing is intentional within the meaning of Article II (a) of the Convention where the perpetrator meant to cause the death of the victim or acted with knowledge that death was a likely consequence of the act or omission. This does not include negligence or gross negligence (citations omitted).

Similarly, the Court found that causing serious bodily or mental harm with general intent involves meaning to cause such harm or knowing that such harm is likely to result from one’s conduct ( para. 334 ). Finally, imposing measures intended to prevent births with general intent involves meaning to prevent births or knowing that one’s conduct is likely to prevent births ( para. 369 ).

In his Declaration, Judge Tladi writes that “the Court acknowledges, in substance, the relevance of dolus eventualis in respect of the actus reus .” The trial judgments cited by the Court found that “killing” as a genocidal act and “murder” as a crime against humanity may involve either dolus directus or dolus eventualis. In common law terms, dolus directus corresponds to direct intent or purpose, while dolus eventualis involves acceptance of foreseen risk analogous to implied malice or depraved indifference (see Stakić ). While the Court does not expressly mention the dolus eventualis element of acceptance of risk (sometimes described as “reconciliation” or “consent”), the formulation it draws from the ILC (knowledge of likely results) is close if not identical in substance.
articles.lede: Analysis of the International Court of Justice's judgment in The Gambia v.

articles.title: Affaire Bossembélé: un témoin met en cause Papy Bozizé dans l’arrestation de six douaniers
articles.description: Les audiences dans l’affaire dite de « Bossembélé » se poursuivent devant la Cour pénale spéciale (CPS) à Bangui. Le 23 novembre, la cour a entendu, sous l’anonymat, un témoin présenté comme victime dans l’affaire de l’arrestation de six douaniers à Bouar, dans la préfecture de la Nana-Mambéré, en 2012. Identifié sous le code BOS-06,…
paragraphs: Identifié sous le code BOS-06, ce témoin affirme avoir été arrêté en 2012 à Bouar avec cinq de ses collègues par Papy Bozizé, fils de l’ancien président François Bozizé, également mis en cause dans cette affaire de crimes contre l’humanité.

À la barre, il a expliqué avoir été interpellé alors qu’il exerçait ses fonctions de douanier, sans jamais connaître les raisons de son arrestation. Selon son témoignage, Papy Bozizé, qui était à l’époque commandant du groupement de la région militaire numéro 3, se substituait aux agents des douanes dans leurs missions. Une situation dont le témoin dit s’être opposé lors d’une opération menée avec ses collègues.

Les six hommes auraient ensuite été conduits à la prison de Bossembélé à bord d’un véhicule bâché. Interrogé par les juges sur une éventuelle connaissance de leur détention par les autorités judiciaires de l’époque, le témoin a répondu par l’affirmative. Il a notamment évoqué les visites régulières du magistrat Éric Tambo, dont l’épouse faisait partie des douaniers arrêtés. « C’est même lui qui avait apporté le document de notre libération », a-t-il déclaré.

Une version contestée par les avocats de la défense. Selon eux, la libération des six douaniers sur instruction de la justice démontre que leurs clients ne sauraient être tenus responsables de leur détention. Le parquet a, pour sa part, soutenu que les autorités judiciaires n’avaient aucune emprise sur la prison civile de Bossembélé à cette époque. Il a également souligné que le régisseur s’y rendait rarement et que les détenus y avaient été transférés sans procès-verbaux d’audition.

Concernant les personnes mises en cause, le témoin a indiqué n’avoir aperçu l’accusé Firmin Junior Danboy qu’à deux reprises, sans connaître ses activités ni la nature de sa mission. Il a également affirmé ne pas connaître Eugène Ngaïkosset et Vianney Semndiro.

En revanche, il s’est dit convaincu que l’ancien président François Bozizé était informé de l’arrestation des six douaniers. Il a notamment décrit la prison de Bossembélé comme étant « la prison des Bozizé ».

Dans cette affaire, les personnes mises en cause sont poursuivies pour des faits de meurtres, de torture, de traitements cruels et dégradants ainsi que de disparitions forcées, constitutifs de crimes contre l’humanité.

articles.title: Centrafrique: à Gordil, les Wagner noirs sèment la terreur et le chaos
articles.description: À Gordile, les miliciens Wagner noirs imposent un racket et sèment la terreur en Centrafrique, écrasant une population totalement démunie.
paragraphs: C’est une descente aux enfers que subissent les habitants de Gordil, dans la préfecture de la Vakaga, face aux agissements des miliciens d’autodéfense surnommés « Wagner noirs ». Dans l’ensemble de la localité et sur tous les axes de circulation, ces hommes imposent leur loi par la force et multiplient les exactions contre les habitants et les travailleurs de la zone. Entre racket décomplexé et abus de pouvoir, ils sèment la terreur et le chaos sur une population laissée sans défense.

Sur le terrain, cette mainmise se traduit d’abord par un système d’extorsion implacable qui paralyse les déplacements quotidiens. Sur les dix kilomètres séparant le chantier aurifère de Mandjam du centre de Gordil, ces hommes ont planté quatre barrières routières sur cinq et extorquent 5 000 francs CFA à chaque moto à chaque passage.

Selon les informations recueillies par la rédaction du CNC, les motocyclistes doivent raquer 5 000 francs CFA à chacune des quatre barrières tenues par les Wagner noirs. Une moto qui traverse les quatre points de contrôle doit ainsi cracher jusqu’à 20 000 francs CFA. Les passagers transportés sont également soumis à des rackets supplémentaires qui plongent les familles dans un profond malaise et une détresse quotidienne.

Sur cet axe de seulement dix kilomètres, les usagers doivent franchir cinq barrières au total. Quatre sont contrôlées par les Wagner noirs et une autre par les soldats des Forces armées centrafricaines ( FACA ). Les populations dénoncent une avalanche de taxes arbitraires qui rend leurs déplacements ruineux et entretient un climat d’insécurité permanente.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: Journée internationale des droits de l’enfant, l’Association Action Solidaire dénonce les promesses sans lendemain et réclame une véritable protection des enfants

Pour justifier ce pillage organisé, les Wagner noirs prétendent qu’ils ne touchent aucun salaire de l’État centrafricain. Ils osent affirmer que le président Faustin-Archange Touadéra ne les paie pas et qu’ils doivent donc se servir eux-mêmes sur le dos des citoyens. Selon leurs excuses bidon, ils seraient les premiers exposés aux risques sur le terrain et auraient le droit de s’enrichir à coups de pressions.
À lire aussi: « La rue a obéi, le pouvoir a puni: quand la ville morte devient le crime d’avoir raison »

Mais à Gordil, ces miliciens ne se contentent plus de jouer les protecteurs. Ils s’imposent sans vergogne dans presque tous les rouages de la vie publique. Au marché, sur les chantiers aurifères et aux barrières routières, ils dictent leurs propres prélèvements. Ils s’arrogent aussi des pouvoirs qui appartiennent normalement à la police, à la gendarmerie, à la douane et à l’administration municipale, faisant régner leur loi arbitraire.

La présence des FACA dans la localité ne pèse pas lourd face à cet état de fait. Sur le terrain, ce sont les Wagner noirs qui font la pluie et le beau temps. Leur chef local est connu sous le nom de Didier. Ces miliciens d’autodéfense, formés par le groupe Wagner pour soi-disant protéger les populations contre les groupes armés, sont aujourd’hui pointés du doigt par des habitants pour multiplier les rackets et les exactions contre ceux qu’ils prétendent défendre.
articles.lede: À Gordile, les miliciens Wagner noirs imposent un racket et sèment la terreur en Centrafrique, écrasant une population totalement démunie.

articles.title: Five women killed every hour by partners or family members
articles.description: Some 47,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025 – five every hour – according to new UN figures published on Tuesday.
paragraphs: Nearly one in three women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence, yet only seven per cent report it to police, a separate UN Women report finds.
Together, the two reports reveal violence that is widespread, largely hidden and rarely punished – and women steadily losing faith in the systems meant to protect them.

The 2026 Femicide Brief, published by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime ( UNODC) and UN Women ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, finds that partners and relatives were behind 60 per cent of the 78,000 intentional killings of women and girls worldwide last year.
For many survivors, reporting abuse can mean risking everything: their homes, children, financial security and even their lives.
Briefing journalists at UN Headquarters in New York, UN Women Deputy Executive Director Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda said women were losing trust in the systems meant to protect them.

“ The silence is getting louder in most countries where we have tracked it over time. Fewer women are seeking help today than before. We are going backwards,” she said. “Our data shows justice systems globally make silence the safest choice a woman can make.”
She urged communities and institutions to believe survivors, whether or not they can provide physical evidence or recall every detail of their abuse.
“It costs nothing to believe someone. And it changes everything to believe a survivor, every single time ,” she said.
UN Women’s report, Access to Justice for Women Survivors of Violence, draws on data from 54 countries and traces the barriers women face from seeking help to navigating the courts.
articles.lede: Some 47,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025 – five every hour – according to new UN figures published on Tuesday.

Bangladesh: the impossible police reform?
articles.description: Acting as a tool for repression during the Awami League rule and its violent crackdown of the 2004 protests, the Bangladeshi police is in dire need of reform but the changes are small and the laws are stalled.
paragraphs: No institution was more deeply implicated in the state violence that swept Bangladesh between July 16 th and August 5 th, 2024 than its police force. Most of the roughly 900 protesters and bystanders killed in that period died from gun fire by state security forces, and the police were foremost among them.

The UN human rights office (OHCHR), in its fact-finding report, concluded that the police, together with paramilitary state security forces, had “resorted to use of force violations against protesters, including systematic and widespread extrajudicial killings as part of a coordinated strategy of repression”.

The police were also at the heart of the mass arrest campaign of late July, which included night-time “block raids” on whole neighbourhoods which resulted in more than 11,700 arrests between July 1 st and 4 August 4 th, 2024.

On the police side, officers were targeted by mob violence as protestors responded to police gunfire: two policemen were beaten to death in the capital, Dhaka, on July 19 th, and 15 others were killed in an attack on a police station in the district of Sirajganj on August 4 th.

When the Awami League Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina fled the country on August 5 th, 2024 crowds attacked and burned police stations across the country, and officers were lynched in several places, where police had earlier fired on crowds.

According to the police, 44 officers were killed during the protest period, and 450 of the country’s 639 police stations were destroyed or damaged. For days afterwards, officers were too frightened to report for duty and the force effectively ceased to function for at least a week, with students in Dhaka stepping in as traffic police just to keep the capital city’s streets moving. Faith in the police was also at an all time low.

The police’s violent suppression of the 2024 protests was the most extreme episode, but it was not an aberration. For fifteen years, the force had been the Awami League government’s principal instrument of repression.

Police filed mass cases against opposition activists, made arbitrary arrests and tortured detainees on remand. Its specialised unit, the Detective Branch, was implicated in enforced disappearances, and so-called “ crossfire” killings. In 2018, according to an inquiry set up after Hasina’s fall, the police were among the state agencies used to rig the general elections. And this was not unique to the Awami League: “crossfire” killings and torture in custody were widespread when the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) was in power between 2001 and 2006.

The fall of the Awami League and the installation of an interim government led by Muhammad Yunus therefore created what looked like a rare opening for serious police reform. “The need for police reform was not specifically related to August 2024,” Baharul Alam, the inspector general of police (IGP) appointed after the fall of the Awami League, points out to Justice Info. “It has been a need felt for a long time. It was just felt more after August 2024.”
articles.lede: Acting as a tool for repression during the Awami League rule and its violent crackdown of the 2004 protests, the Bangladeshi police is in dire need of reform but the changes are small and the laws are stalled.

articles.title: Egypt: Authorities must reverse decision to close Mada Masr and drop all charges against its editor in chief Lina Attalah
articles.description: Ahead of an appeal hearing on 25 November against the closure of Mada Masr and the conviction of its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah for operating a website without a license Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Sara Hashash, said: “Egyptian authorities have an opportunity to change course and meet their…
paragraphs: “Egyptian authorities have an opportunity to change course and meet their international obligations by reversing this disgraceful decision to shut down Mada Masr. The latest escalation against Mada Masr is a chilling signal of the Egyptian authorities’ resolve to silence independent journalism and eradicate any critical reporting that challenges the official narrative or scrutinizes their human rights record or other conduct. Egyptian authorities must immediately end their brazen assault on press freedom, quash the closure order against Mada Masr– one of the few remaining lifelines for independent information about Egypt.

“The authorities should also drop all charges against Lina Attalah who faces trial in a separate case, on charges of publishing false news and operating a website without a licence, for which she could be sentenced to up to one year in prison.
The latest escalation against Mada Masr is a chilling signal of the Egyptian authorities’ resolve to silence independent journalism

“The successive criminal proceedings against Lina Attalah and Mada Masr are part of a broader escalating crackdown aimed at extinguishing independent reporting in Egypt and intimidating independent media into silence. Lina Attalah and her colleagues have faced six politically motivated criminal prosecutions for their reporting in the past six years. Mada Masr has repeatedly sought to obtain a license since 2018 and to operate in full transparency. The authorities should grant Mada the license they have sought for years.

“These alarming developments must be met with a strong international response. The international community, including allies of Egypt, such as the European Union, must press the authorities to end their crackdown on media freedom and ensure that journalists and human rights defenders can carry out their work free from intimidation, harassment and fear of reprisals.”

On 27 October, a court convicted Lina Attalah in her capacity as editor in chief of Mada Masr of operating a website without a license, imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (54,467 USD) and ordered Mada Masr’s closure and the seizure of its property. The judge handed down the sentence in the first and only hearing after an expedited trial that took place just five days after the referral. In blatant violation of defence rights, the judge refused the defence’s request to adjourn the session to give lawyers adequate time to prepare their defence and refused their request to submit additional documentation or to summon witnesses. Lina Attalah was [detained at the court for hours until the fine was paid on the same day. The appeal hearing against this ruling is scheduled for 25 November 2026.

The same judge was assigned to the other trial in which Lina Attalah faces charges of publishing false news and operating a website without a licence, but her defence requested the recusal of the judge. Another court will decide on the defence’s request for the judge to recuse himself on 26 November.
articles.lede: “Egyptian authorities have an opportunity to change course and meet their international obligations by reversing this disgraceful decision to shut down Mada Masr.

EU: Forced Labor Remedies Should Center on Workers
articles.description: Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions said in a report released today.
paragraphs: (Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions said in a report released today.

In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

“Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” said Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”

The groups propose concrete steps for companies to prepare, deliver and assess their remediation obligations. The report comes as the European Union prepares to enforce its Forced Labour Regulation, which will ban products made with forced labor from the EU market across all sectors and stages of production beginning on December 14, 2027. Under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, companies in its scope will also have a legal duty to remedy harm they cause, completely or in part.

Academics and experts found that forced labor is rarely only the result of a few bad actors, but is rooted in poverty, discrimination, weak labor protections, and restrictive migration regimes. Migrant workers face heightened risks, including recruitment fees that lead to debt bondage, deceptive recruitment practices, and visas tied to a single employer. Fear of deportation and retaliation often keeps victims from seeking redress.

The civil society groups said that companies should put in place remediation measures that restore as much as possible the situation for workers if the abuse had not occurred. This would require the cessation of the abuse, restitution, rehabilitation, compensation, apologies, and guarantees of non-repetition. Companies should also ensure that workers and their representatives can identify abuses through grievance mechanisms they trust, define remedies, and assess whether they have been delivered to their satisfaction, the groups said. At all times, affected workers should be protected from retaliation.

Companies should treat remediation as part of their human rights due diligence, not as a one-off response to a scandal, the groups said. Their responsibility should reflect their involvement in failing to prevent or meaningfully address the harm. Companies should not “cut and run” from suppliers when and where labor abuses, including forced labor, is found, as this can leave workers worse off. Instead, the groups said, companies should fairly agree on how to address and share remediation costs.

To prevent forced labor from occurring and recurring, companies should examine structural causes such as poverty, discrimination and impairments to freedom of association but also how their own purchasing practices may drive it. They should pay to cover the cost of decent working conditions and living wages. The groups point to worker-driven models, such as the Fair Food Program in US agriculture and the Dindigul Agreement in India’s textile sector, as evidence of good practices.

Centrafrique: à Sam-Ouandja, l’hôpital général transformé en hôtel payant, une vieille malade abandonnée dans ses excréments jusqu’à sa mort
articles.description: À l'hôpital Sam-Ouandja en Centrafrique, les patients subissent une tarification abusive et des négligences tragiques. Découvrez l'enquête exclusive.
paragraphs: À Sam-Ouandja, dans la Haute-Kotto, une enquête du CNC révèle des pratiques de facturation contestées et de graves négligences envers les malades.

L’hôpital de Sam-Ouandja, dans la préfecture de la Haute-Kotto, fait l’objet de graves témoignages recueillis par la rédaction du CNC. Un bâtiment construit grâce au financement du Programme des Nations unies pour le développement (PNUD) est désormais soumis à une tarification journalière imposée aux patients hospitalisés. Plus grave encore, une femme âgée est morte dans des conditions particulièrement troublantes, après avoir été abandonnée sur son lit, sans assistance suffisante, selon les informations recueillies au cours de notre enquête.

À Sam-Ouandja, petite localité de la Haute-Kotto où une grande partie de la population vit de l’agriculture, l’accès aux soins représente déjà une difficulté pour de nombreuses familles. La construction d’un nouveau bâtiment hospitalier, financée par le PNUD, devait contribuer à améliorer les conditions d’accueil et d’hospitalisation.
À lire aussi: VAKAGA: après l’assassinat crapuleux de quatre Wagner noirs par les mercenaires russes, que dit Gilbert Toumou Déya, ex-chef rebelle et initiateur de ces milices à Birao?
Le bâtiment est de dimensions modestes, mais sa construction représente un progrès pour cet établissement sanitaire. Les malades peuvent désormais être accueillis dans des locaux plus adaptés.
À lire aussi: David Gbéti: « Les décrets présidentiels ne servent plus à rien dans ce pays où chacun fait ce qu’il veut sous le regard passif des autorités »

Seulement, les investigations menées sur place par l’équipe du CNC font état d’une pratique qui pénalise les patients. Le médecin responsable de l’établissement a instauré, selon les témoignages recueillis, un paiement journalier pour les personnes hospitalisées dans ce nouveau bâtiment.
À lire aussi: Sécurité nationale: expropriation pour cause d’utilité publique sur l’avenue des Martyrs, une vraie nécessité militaire?

Autrement dit, chaque journée passée dans ces locaux entraîne une somme supplémentaire à régler. Le montant exact de cette tarification reste à documenter, tout comme son fondement administratif et sa destination.
À lire aussi: Marche pacifique du 13 novembre: capitulation du gouvernement et volte-face du ministre Zokoué sous la pression des opposants
articles.lede: À l'hôpital Sam-Ouandja en Centrafrique, les patients subissent une tarification abusive et des négligences tragiques. Découvrez l'enquête exclusive.

articles.title: Landmines: New Use, Production Undermine Ban Treaty
articles.description: New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020.
paragraphs: (Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch said today with the release of the “ Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines. Human Rights Watch is a founding member of the campaign and contributed to the report.

The 200-page report examines global compliance with the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty and the challenges facing the treaty nearly three decades after its adoption. The treaty comprehensively bans antipersonnel mines and commits countries to eliminate stockpiled weapons, clear contaminated land, and assist mine victims and affected communities.

“At a time when civilian casualties are rising and new technologies make mines easier to deploy, supporting the Mine Ban Treaty is more important than ever,” said Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “All countries should join the treaty, and members should fully uphold its obligations.”

Antipersonnel mines continue to kill and maim civilians long after fighting moves elsewhere. Whether they are placed by soldiers on the ground or delivered remotely by weapons systems and drones, the mines contaminate land, roads, and communities for years. Their presence can prevent displaced families from returning home, obstruct humanitarian operations, and undermine efforts to rebuild livelihoods and food production.

A total of 162 countries are now bound by the Mine Ban Treaty. Three countries joined during the reporting period: Lebanon, Marshall Islands, and Tonga. Five other countries withdrew from the treaty in 2025 and 2026: Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland.

Ukraine announced on July 18, 2025, that it would “suspend the operation” of the treaty while engaged in armed conflict with Russia, citing Russia’s extensive use of landmines. Suspensions, however, are unlawful under the treaty, notably during armed conflict, and Ukraine remains fully bound by all the treaty’s obligations. During the reporting period, Ukraine has acquired, produced, and used newly assembled antipersonnel mines, including types that are delivered by drone, in violation of the treaty.
In addition to Ukraine’s use of antipersonnel mines, states not party to the treaty used them, including Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, and Russia.

Antipersonnel mines were increasingly used in border conflicts, involving Cambodia and Thailand, Bangladesh and Myanmar, and in Thailand along the borders with Myanmar and Malaysia. Non-state armed groups also used antipersonnel mines, in many cases improvised, in Colombia, India, Myanmar, Pakistan, Sudan, and in locations in Western and Central Africa, including in the Chad Basin, Burkina Faso, and Mali.

The Landmine Monitor reported that 15 states not party to the treaty either currently produce antipersonnel mines or maintain the option to produce them in the future. Of these, India, Myanmar, Poland, Russia, and South Korea appear to be actively producing or developing antipersonnel mines. Finland, Latvia, and Lithuania—all of which withdrew from the treaty in 2025—have indicated their intent to develop or acquire antipersonnel mines. Non-state armed groups have produced improvised mines that explode due to the presence, proximity, or contact of a person in Colombia, India, Africa’s Sahel region, and sporadically in Thailand.
articles.lede: New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020.

articles.title: EJIL: The Podcast! Episode 48: Holding a state responsible for genocide: Gambia v Myanmar before the ICJ
articles.description: The ICJ’s judgment in Gambia v Myanmar has been eagerly received, not least in the Cox’s Bazaar camp where Rohingya survivors watched live as judgment was rendered. The Genocide Convention gives t…
paragraphs: The ICJ’s judgment in Gambia v Myanmar has been eagerly received, not least in the Cox’s Bazaar camp where Rohingya survivors watched live as judgment was rendered. The Genocide Convention gives the ICJ jurisdiction in cases of alleged genocide which it does not enjoy in respect of other atrocity crimes (like crimes against humanity and war crimes), meaning approaches to genocide shape the availability of international judicial redress for many victimised groups worldwide. Gambia v Myanmar also has implications for current proceedings brought by South Africa against Israel in respect of Gaza, and for third states weighing their own obligations under the Convention to prevent genocide elsewhere. International lawyers are thus poring over the majority judgment (9 justices), the joint dissenting opinion (6 justices: Vice-President Sebutinde, Judges Tomka, Abraham, Xue, Nolte and Judge ad hoc Kress), and a further 16 opinions and declarations.

In this episode, Marko Milanovic explores some key issues in the case with Adil Haque (Distinguished Professor of Law and Judge Jon O. Newman Scholar at Rutgers Law School) and Mona Rishmawi (currently a member of the UN Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan, formerly Executive Director of the UN International Commission of Inquiry on Darfur and a veteran UN OHCHR official with experience in Syria, Sri Lanka, Iraq and the Occupied Palestinian Territory).
The conversation opens with overall evaluations of the judgment (minute 00:01:18) before touching on:
Mike Becker, ‘ Recent developments in reliance upon third-party fact-finding at the International Court of Justice ’ (2025) 38(3) Leiden Journal of International Law 617-640
Marko’s recent EJIL:Talk! post, ‘Did the Court Change its Approach to Defining or Proving Genocidal Intent’: Part I and Part II

Adil Haque’s posts on Just Security, ‘ Proving Genocide: Patterns of Conduct ’ (8 Jan 2026); ‘ Elements of Genocide: Intent to Kill’ (9 Jan 2026; cited in Declaration of Judge Tladi); ‘ Proving Genocide: Party Presentation ’ (14 Jan 2026); ‘ Proving Genocide: The Burden of Proof’ (23 Jan 2026); ‘Proving Genocide: Genocidal Intent and Other Aims’, (25 Feb 2026); ‘ Genocide and Intent to Kill Revisited ’ (23 July 2026); ‘ The ICJ Finds that Myanmar Committed Genocide against the Rohingya: A Preliminary Analysis ’ (19 Nov 2026)

Marco Longobardo, ‘ The Monetary Gold Principle and States’ Obligations Triggered by a Serious Risks of Atrocities Being Committed by Another State: The Cases of the Duty to Prevent Genocide and the Duty to Ensure Respect for IHL ’ (2025) 27(3) International Community Law Review 282–329
Paola Gaeta & Giulia Pinzauti (eds), (2026) 24(3) Journal of International Criminal Justice symposium on ‘ Genocide in War ’
Kevin Heller, ‘ The Relationship between IHL and Genocide in the Gambia v Myanmar Case ’ (21 Nov 2026)
articles.lede: The ICJ’s judgment in Gambia v Myanmar has been eagerly received, not least in the Cox’s Bazaar camp where Rohingya survivors watched live as judgment was rendered.

paragraphs: Lors d’un débat diffusé sur les ondes de la radio Ndeke Luka consacré aux exactions sur les voies de transport, les parlementaires et les représentants de la société civile ont mis en lumière la gravité des exactions commises aux postes de contrôle. Jordan Badengbé, acteur de la société civile, a rejoint l’alerte lancée par plusieurs députés pour dénoncer le comportement de certains agents des forces de l’ordre face aux usagers.

Au-delà des prélèvements financiers illicites, Jordan Badengbé a souligné que les citoyens subissent au quotidien des humiliations, des intimidations ainsi que des agressions physiques et verbales lorsqu’ils osent contester les sommes exigées. Ces pratiques, répétées le long des corridors routiers, créent un climat de terreur chez les conducteurs de moto-taxis, les commerçants et les simples voyageurs.
À lire aussi: Affaire du passeport de Dologuélé: Jean-Pierre Mara propose d’en faire un sujet de thèse de doctorat à l’Université de Bangui

Cette prise de position fait écho aux dénonciations portées par les représentants du peuple à l’Assemblée nationale, à l’image de Suzanne Saté pour la Ouaka ou de Silvestre Dongombe pour Bégoua. Les élus ont rappelé que les contrôles routiers doivent s’effectuer dans le respect de la dignité humaine et des règles républicaines, loin des abus de pouvoir constatés sur le terrain.
À lire aussi: L’affaire de passeport confisqué: Anicet Georges Dologuélé dénonce une gestion familiale de l’État par le clan Touadéra

Face à ces révélations, Jordan Badengbé et les députés demandent au gouvernement d’agir avec fermeté. Ils exigent non seulement le démantèlement des barrières clandestines, mais aussi des sanctions disciplinaires et judiciaires exemplaires contre les agents coupables d’actes de violence, afin de restaurer la confiance entre la population et les forces de défense et de sécurité.
À lire aussi: Opération commando de Wagner dans le Haut-Mbomou: la recherche de la sous-préfète de Bambouti tourne à la démonstration de force au village Ngouyo
Les exactions routières ont atteint un niveau alarmant, avec des agents des forces de l’ordre impliqués dans des actes de violence qui menacent la sécurité des citoyens.
Note: les deux premiers groupes sont réservés uniquement aux publications officielles du CNC
articles.lede: Urgence d'agir contre la violence physique et verbale sur les axes routiers. Découvrez les exigences de Jordan Badengbé et des députés.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Genocide Ruling Tests International Accountability
Centrafrique: à Bimbo, un homme soupçonné d’avoir empoisonné son épouse, ses quatre enfants et sa belle-mère
articles.description: La gendarmerie de Bimbo arrête un homme après l'empoisonnement mortel de son épouse, ses quatre enfants et sa belle-mère en Centrafrique.
paragraphs: Un homme a été arrêté dimanche à Bimbo, après la mort de six membres de sa famille, dont son épouse, ses quatre enfants et sa belle-mère. Les victimes auraient consommé un jus mélangé à une substance toxique, selon les premières informations recueillies par les enquêteurs.

Le suspect a été placé à la disposition de la gendarmerie de Bimbo. Les corps des six victimes ont été transférés à la morgue, tandis que les circonstances exactes de ce drame restent à établir par une enquête sérieuse.

À Bimbo, dans son quartier et sur les réseaux sociaux, des informations circulent sur les motivations qui auraient conduit l’homme à commettre cet acte. Selon certains témoignages, il aurait voulu acquérir une magie noire. Des personnes affirment que des individus présentés comme des gourous de la magie noire lui auraient demandé de sacrifier plusieurs membres de sa famille en échange de ces pouvoirs.
D’autres habitants rejettent cette explication et estiment qu’aucune croyance mystique ne peut justifier l’empoisonnement de sa propre épouse, de ses enfants et de sa belle-mère.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: Radio Lengo Songo, RT, Sputnik et l’IA Claude au cœur d’une vaste opération d’influence pro-russe

Si les faits sont confirmés, il s’agirait d’un acte criminel d’une extrême gravité. L’idée qu’un homme puisse décider de faire mourir six membres de sa famille pour obtenir des pouvoirs qui ne peuvent durer que quelques mois ou années dépasse l’entendement.

L’enquête de la gendarmerie devra établir les circonstances de l’empoisonnement, identifier la substance utilisée et déterminer les véritables motivations du suspect. Pour l’heure, aucune conclusion définitive ne peut être tirée sur les raisons de ce drame familial.
Les enquêteurs de la gendarmerie de Bimbo poursuivent leurs investigations pour identifier la substance toxique utilisée lors de cet empoisonnement mortel qui a décimé une famille entière.
Note: les deux premiers groupes sont réservés uniquement aux publications officielles du CNC
articles.lede: La gendarmerie de Bimbo arrête un homme après l'empoisonnement mortel de son épouse, ses quatre enfants et sa belle-mère en Centrafrique.
