Le dictateur de Bangui, Faustin-Archange Touadera, prisonnier des groupes armés: un gouvernement de rebelles et de criminels pour la 7ème République?
articles.description: Écouter l'articleTélécharger En Centrafrique, la formation du prochain gouvernement ressemble à une reddition masquée sous les apparences de la paix. Le
paragraphs: En Centrafrique, la formation du prochain gouvernement ressemble à une reddition masquée sous les apparences de la paix. Le pouvoir reste captif d’anciens belligérants qui imposent leurs conditions depuis des années. Cette emprise ne date pas d’hier, malheureusement, les centrafricains assistent depuis des années à la formation successive de gouvernement de rebelles.

Dès 2003, les accords successifs ont ouvert la porte aux chefs de factions armées dans les sphères dirigeantes. Khartoum en 2019 n’a fait qu’amplifier ce mécanisme déjà bien rodé. Chaque signature renforce leur emprise.

La Constitution interdit pourtant formellement l’entrée au gouvernement de personnes issues de la violence armée. Mais ces textes écrits semblent peser moins lourd que les engagements verbaux ou signés sous la menace. Le chef de l’État se retrouve ligoté par ses propres promesses.

Les groupes armés ne se contentent plus d’attendre des postes. Ils exigent, menacent et fractionnent leurs mouvements pour multiplier les revendications. Cette tactique dilue toute résistance sérieuse de l’État central. Bangui plie à chaque nouvelle exigence.

Paul Crescent Beninga l’explique sans ambages sur les ondes: nommer un responsable rebelle ministre revient à récompenser la kalachnikov plutôt que le mérite ou l’honnêteté. Le message envoyé au pays entier devient limpide.

Joseph Bindoumi va plus loin: ces accords ressemblent à des armistices déguisés, où l’État reconnaît sa défaite face aux armes. Il refuse d’associer la Ligue des droits de l’homme à de telles signatures. Le peuple doit entendre ce refus.

Alexis N’dui Yabela parle de coutume constitutionnelle née des pratiques répétées. Les accords politiques s’ajoutent à la Constitution comme une couche parallèle. Cette superposition rend les interdictions écrites presque inopérantes.

Les mêmes noms reviennent dans les rumeurs qui circulent à Bangui. Des chefs de factions, connus depuis 2008, figurent déjà sur les listes qui passent de main en main. La logique qui prévaut n’a rien à voir avec le développement ou la reconstruction.

Les forces de défense nationales restent en marge de ces tractations. On préfère encore discuter avec ceux qui tiennent les armes plutôt que de leur faire face avec des moyens propres. L’État continue de marchander sa propre autorité.
À mesure que l’investiture approche, les listes s’affinent. Des noms de 3R, d’UPC, de CPC apparaissent en bonne place. Les citoyens observent ce ballet incessant de concessions.
articles.lede: En Centrafrique, la formation du prochain gouvernement ressemble à une reddition masquée sous les apparences de la paix. Le pouvoir reste captif d’anciens belligérants qui imposent leurs conditions depuis des années.

articles.title: Croatia: Border Pushbacks of Adults, Children Violate Rights
articles.description: Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite EU efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today
paragraphs: (Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today.

The 43-page report, “Doing Europe’s Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina,” finds that Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks, often violently. An EU-funded Croatian border monitoring program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks. Instead, the EU has increased funding to Croatia for border management without addressing the abuse at the border.
Annex: Unofficial Translation of the Croatia Ministry of Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch
Croatia Ministry of the Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch (Original Email in Croatian)

“Violent pushbacks by Croatian police are a continuing issue, affecting children as well as adults, and the EU-funded systems set up to curb them aren’t working,” said Michael Garcia Bochenek, senior children’s rights counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The EU needs to act to ensure that Croatia respects EU law and protects the rights of those at its borders.”

Human Rights Watch interviewed more than 80 people, including seven unaccompanied children, four children travelling with family members, and six parents travelling with their children, and also interviewed 15 aid workers and others who offer information and other support to asylum seekers and migrants.

People interviewed said that Croatian police beat or kicked them, took all their money, and confiscated or destroyed their phones. In some cases, people said, the border police seized their documents, took their shoes, or even forced them to strip to their underwear before pushing them back across the border.

“We told them that we are a family, but [the Croatian police] still took my husband away in one van and me and my daughters in another,” said a woman from Ghana. “We were separated for two days from my husband. They pushed me and my daughters to Bosnia through the woods. No phone, no food, no water. We were walking all day. We were lost and scared for many hours.”

Croatian authorities demonstrate official tolerance for unlawful police pushbacks through inadequate oversight, ineffective investigations and a lack of meaningful accountability, and repeated minimization—and often outright denial—of these practices, Human Rights Watch found. The government has not prosecuted any police officers for taking part in pushbacks, even in cases in which people suffered serious injuries or extreme forms of humiliation. Seven officers received disciplinary sanctions for mistreatment of migrants between 2020 and 2025, the Croatian Interior Ministry told Human Rights Watch.

The only accommodation option in Bosnia and Herzegovina for most people pushed back from Croatia, including unaccompanied children and families with children, is the Lipa Migrant Reception Centre, 25 kilometres from Bihać, the nearest city. The center has experienced water shortages and power outages and has no local bus service. Healthcare services are limited, and the center provides no education for children.
articles.lede: (Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice…

articles.title: Assemblée nationale 2022: quand le rapport accablant révélait 500 millions détournés et un réseau mafieux dans la solde
articles.description: Écouter l'articleTélécharger En octobre 2022, la Commission Spéciale de Comptabilité et de Contrôle de l’Assemblée nationale rendait un rapport explosif
paragraphs: Trois ans plus tard, ce rapport mérite d’être rappelé. Car face à ces révélations accablantes, l’Assemblée nationale a choisi de sanctionner cinq petits agents techniques de la Commission d’Attribution des Marchés pour “mauvaise manière de servir” et “intelligence avec autrui en vue du détournement de deniers publics”. Pendant ce temps, les véritables responsables des détournements massifs documentés en 2022 n’ont jamais été inquiétés.

La Commission Spéciale, présidée par l’Honorable Anatole Ndemagouda-Gbagot, a travaillé de juin à octobre 2022 dans des conditions extrêmement difficiles. Pas de salle de travail, pas de moyens financiers au départ, et surtout, une obstruction planifiée de ceux qui avaient le plus à cacher.

Le Directeur Général des Finances Nganazouï Rameau Christ et le Chef de Service de la Pairie ont refusé catégoriquement de fournir les documents comptables: sorties de caisse, factures, programmes d’emploi. Malgré “de nombreuses correspondances” au Directeur, au payeur, et même trois lettres au Président de l’Assemblée nationale, rien n’a été fait.

La Commission écrit dans son rapport: “La rétention des documents comptables par le Directeur Général des Finances, du Matériel et de la Logistique et le Chef de Service de la Pairie constitue une faute lourde et mérite une sanction conformément aux textes en vigueur”. Pourtant, ces deux responsables n’ont jamais été sanctionnés.

Et ce n’est pas tout! Sur le plan de l’évacuations sanitaires, 113 millions partent en fumée sans justificatifs. Le rapport démontre que sur un budget de 80 millions de francs CFA pour les évacuations sanitaires, 113,4 millions ont été dépensés, soit un dépassement de 142%. L’argent a été décaissé, mais aucun document justificatif n’a été fourni à la Commission: pas de billets d’avion, pas de copies de passeport, pas de bulletins d’admission ou de sortie d’hôpital.

Plus scandaleux encore: une évacuation sanitaire a été accordée à l’enfant d’un personnel, en l’occurrence le payeur lui-même. Les textes réglementaires prévoient que les évacuations sanitaires sont réservées aux députés et au personnel, pas à leurs descendants. Cette violation flagrante n’a entraîné aucune sanction.

Plus grave encore, des missions fantômes, avec 75 millions de dépassement dans le budget. Sur les missions parlementaires, le rapport documente un chaos total. La questure a fusionné les frais de missions et les frais de transport dans son rapport pour masquer les irrégularités. La Commission a découvert un écart de 3,4 millions de francs CFA correspondant à une mission du Président de l’Assemblée nationale qui n’était même pas mentionnée dans le rapport de la questure.

Pour les missions extérieures, le dépassement atteint 75,5 millions de francs CFA. Pire: la Commission a découvert des “missions payées sans appel de fonds” pour un montant de 2,98 millions de francs. Comment peut-on payer des missions sans avoir émis d’appel de fonds? Personne n’a expliqué ce mystère.

Pendant ce temps, “certains députés et personnel qui ont effectué des missions” attendent toujours que leurs frais leur soient versés. L’argent a été décaissé, mais n’est pas arrivé aux bénéficiaires légitimes.
articles.lede: Trois ans plus tard, ce rapport mérite d’être rappelé.

articles.title: Ethiopia: Lethal artillery strikes on civilian neighbourhoods in Tigray’s Alamata city must be investigated as war crimes
articles.description: For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants.
paragraphs: Artillery attacks by Ethiopia’s military and its allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) that killed dozens of civilians and injured many more in the city of Alamata in the northern region of Tigray, between 26 and 28 September, must be investigated as possible war crimes, Amnesty International said today.

The organization also found that forces affiliated to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), put civilians in harm’s way by establishing military bases in populated residential areas, including in several schools in Alamata, prior to the outbreak of renewed fighting in the region.
The Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) and its TPF allies seized control of the strategic city of Alamata, a key supply hub for troops, food, and fuel, from the TPLF on 28 September.

“For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants. The use of artillery, a weapon with wide-area effects, in densely populated neighbourhoods has a terrible impact on civilians. Indiscriminate attacks violate the rules of international humanitarian law, and these strikes must be investigated as war crimes,” said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International’s Senior Director, Regional Human Rights Impact.
“For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants.

Amnesty International investigated four incidents of artillery shelling on Alamata by the ENDF and TPF between 26 and 28 September and independently verified the deaths of 14 civilians in these attacks. Researchers interviewed 28 individuals, including survivors, witnesses, relatives of victims, humanitarian and medical personnel. Amnesty International’s Evidence Lab analysed eight videos and 17 photographs, as well as satellite imagery of the site and other open-source information.
All names and identifying details have been withheld or changed to protect interviewees who requested anonymity.

Amnesty International wrote to the ENDF, TPF, and TPLF on 27 October, requesting information about these incidents. On 17 November, the organization shared its investigation findings with the ENDF and TPF and invited their comments. ENDF and TPF had not provided a response as at the time of publication.

The use of artillery, a weapon with wide-area effects, in densely populated neighbourhoods has a terrible impact on civilians. Indiscriminate attacks violate the rules of international humanitarian law, and these strikes must be investigated as war crimes.
In a four-page letter sent to Amnesty International on 18 November, the TPLF “categorically reject[ed]’’ the allegations made against it.
articles.lede: For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants.

articles.title: Rita Adeline Fekere: « 66 ans d’indépendance, c’est long et les défis pour les femmes sont encore énormes »: pauvreté, violences, manque d’écoles et poids des traditions continuent de freiner les femmes
articles.description: Écouter l'articleTélécharger Soixante-six ans après l’accession de la République centrafricaine à l’indépendance, les femmes restent confrontées à des
paragraphs: Soixante-six ans après l’accession de la République centrafricaine à l’indépendance, les femmes restent confrontées à des obstacles qui limitent leur accès à l’éducation, à l’autonomie économique et aux responsabilités publiques. Rita Adeline Fekere estime que les progrès enregistrés ne suffisent pas encore à combler ces écarts.
La condition des femmes centrafricaines a évolué depuis 1960. Elles sont aujourd’hui présentes dans des secteurs qui leur étaient auparavant difficilement accessibles.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: le préfet de Bamingui-Bangoran menacé par les mercenaires russes: « Ce qui est arrivé à Bilal va vous arriver »

Rita Adeline Fekere cite notamment l’entrepreneuriat, la science, le sport, le commerce, la santé et la politique. Des femmes occupent désormais des fonctions de ministres, de maires, de juges ou encore de scientifiques.
À lire aussi: Affaire Guen: la CPS fixe un nouveau calendrier pour les réquisitions et plaidoiries
À lire aussi: Souveraineté économique: la leçon de courage du Niger face à la démission des autorités centrafricaines

La coordonnatrice de l’Observatoire national de la parité estime que les progrès restent fragiles tant que les obstacles sociaux, économiques et institutionnels continuent de limiter une grande partie des femmes.
À l’occasion du 66ᵉ anniversaire de l’indépendance, Rita Adeline Fekere porte un regard critique sur le chemin parcouru.
Pour elle, le temps écoulé depuis 1960 doit être mis en perspective avec la situation actuelle des femmes.

La République centrafricaine dispose aujourd’hui d’un cadre légal plus favorable. La loi sur la parité adoptée en 2016 constitue notamment une avancée importante. La Constitution de 2023 vient également renforcer le principe d’égalité entre les femmes et les hommes.
articles.lede: Soixante-six ans après l’accession de la République centrafricaine à l’indépendance, les femmes restent confrontées à des obstacles qui limitent leur accès à l’éducation, à l’autonomie économique et aux responsabilités publiques.

articles.title: India: Modi Rule Has Weakened Democratic Institutions
articles.description: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms.
paragraphs: (London) – Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. Indians have increasingly taken to the streets to protest government repression, corruption, and a deeply flawed revision of voter lists.

The 95-page report, “‘ So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?’: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India ,” finds that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing the political opposition, and weaponizing federal investigative agencies for political ends. Human Rights Watch found that the government is also weakening constitutional and statutory bodies, such as the Election Commission, Central Information Commission, the anti-corruption ombudsman, and human rights commissions, and interfering in the judicial branch.

“Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India’s authoritarian slide.”
Human Rights Watch interviewed over 40 lawyers, journalists, activists, researchers, academics, current and former judges, and former government officials between January 2025 and September 2026.

The Modi administration has frequently disregarded parliamentary oversight mechanisms to impose its political agenda. In December 2023, the government adopted a law that entrenched executive control over the appointment of election commissioners and granted them sweeping legal immunity for actions, decisions, or statements made while carrying out their official duties. The law was passed even as opposition members were suspended in unprecedented numbers from both houses for the entire session of the parliament, 100 from Lok Sabha (the House of the People or lower house) and 46 from Rajya Sabha (the Council of States or upper house).

The BJP did not have a majority in the Rajya Sabha from 2014 to 2024. While all bills must be approved by both houses to become law, some regulating financial matters can be introduced in the Lok Sabha as “money bills,” which do not require Rajya Sabha approval. The Modi administration aggressively used money bills to push through laws with serious consequences for fundamental rights that would not qualify as money bills.

In 2019, the government used this approach to amend the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, significantly expanding the authority of the Enforcement Directorate, the federal enforcement agency it has used to improperly target political opponents, activists, and critics. The expansion of Enforcement Directorate powers would not appear to fall within the parameters set out for a money bill.
articles.lede: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government has systematically weakened institutions established to protect human rights and democratic freedoms.

COP31 Failed Climate-Displaced Communities
articles.description: Leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process.
paragraphs: Leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process. The conference ended without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact—the overarching political agreement for the COP31 climate summit.

I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story. “Walande… the birthplace written in my passport, no longer exists,” he told a hushed room. “It is submerged beneath the waves.” His words moved the high-level event’s moderator to tears.

COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande —and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own. Despite coordinated calls from civil society, related outcome decisions do not include explicit discussion of displacement and planned relocation, and governments failed to increase funding to help frontline communities adapt. Nor was there recognition of the International Court of Justice’s landmark opinion affirming that governments have human rights obligations to address the climate crisis.

I leave Antalya holding both heartbreak and hope: the summit remains a vital space for global solidarity. Alongside partners in the Coalition on Dignified Climate Relocation, we brought frontline leaders, policymakers, and funders together to exchange lessons, and push for rights-respecting national policies and increased funding for communities forced to relocate. After watching our immersive documentary Solwata, several government officials and climate fund directors stepped up, committing to support finance and policies for relocating communities.

Official negotiations fell woefully short, and the UN policy process failed to meet the moment in Antalya. But Marshall Islands, Bangladesh, Fiji, Nepal and other forward-thinking governments are proving that another path is possible. Dignified, rights-respecting solutions already exist—and they can be scaled up.

Ethiopia, as host of COP32, should learn lessons from Australia and Türkiye’s failures, and center efforts to advance finance for adaptation and loss damage which are vital to protect the rights of climate displaced communities.
articles.lede: Leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process.

articles.title: Algorithmic Friction and the Illusion of Positive Control
articles.description: AI models, including decision-support systems, can make the exercise of command control increasingly difficult.
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence (AI) models, including decision-support systems, can make the exercise of command increasingly difficult. A human approval of action records authorization, but does not by itself establish that the commander understood the recommendation, had a meaningful opportunity to evaluate it, or could stop its execution. Preserving those capacities should be a design requirement for military decision-support systems, established before they reach the battlefield.

At the same time, the operational demand for speed is real. In 2020, the Army described Project Convergence demonstrations intended to connect sensors and weapons within twenty seconds of target detection. Accelerating the targeting process can protect friendly forces and exploit fleeting battlefield opportunities. But time saved in collecting and transmitting information should also be available for judgment. A system that consumes every saved second by demanding an earlier decision may improve transmission speed while impoverishing command.

Consider a hypothetical. During an armed conflict, a coalition surveillance swarm detects a convoy approaching a village. One vehicle in the convoy resembles an enemy logistics truck. Other vehicles and nearby buildings may be civilian objects. An automated system fuses the swarm’s imagery with an electronic signature, identifies a probable military target, and recommends a weapon and method of attack. The commander receives a 94 percent confidence score and a twenty-second engagement window.

What does the “94 percent” score describe? Confidence that the object is a truck, that it belongs to an enemy unit, or that the proposed attack is lawful? Are the imagery and electronic signature independent sources, or has one uncertain observation been counted twice? Does the civilian-harm estimate reflect current traffic? The display offers a recommendation. The commander needs to know the grounds for it.

In one version of the scenario, an analyst has already examined the swarm’s imagery, reconciled conflicting information, and identified the remaining uncertainty. The commander knows the mission, understands the anticipated military advantage, and can alter or reject the recommendation. Twenty seconds may be sufficient to complete a judgment substantially prepared beforehand.

In another version, the system delivers the same recommendation without that preparation. The underlying evidence is difficult to retrieve, the clock is counting down, and the interface makes approval easy while requiring several steps to question the result. The commander can authorize action but lacks the ability to reasonably resolve questions that matter before the opportunity expires. The formal allocation of authority is identical. The practical capacity to exercise it is not.

This is the illusion of positive control: an arrangement that preserves the outward appearance of human command while weakening its substance. Both commanders are “in the loop,” however, treating that label as a binary safeguard (human present or absent) conceals the difference between them. Human participation has value only if the person can understand the recommendation, assess it, and influence the outcome. The hypothetical sets no minimum lawful deliberation time. It asks whether the decision process preserves the practical capacity to meet the law’s existing requirements. That is where the legal analysis must begin.
articles.lede: AI models, including decision-support systems, can make the exercise of command control increasingly difficult.

Azerbaijan Further Tightens Grip on Civil Society
articles.description: Azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose new registration requirements, and further restrict their operations. The following day, a court sentenced prominent rights defender Bashir Suleymanli to seven and a half years in prison, the latest in a series of harsh sentences against civil society activists prosecuted over foreign funding.
paragraphs: The proposed legislation would allow authorities, rather than courts, to suspend NGOs for up to a year for broadly defined violations, including failure to meet transparency and anti-money laundering requirements. It would also expand grounds for court-ordered dissolution to include activities deemed a threat to the “legally protected interests of the state and society”—vague standards open to abuse.

Existing NGOs would have just 30 days after the law takes effect to revise their charters and apply for re-registration. The minimum capital to establish a nonprofit foundation, a type of nongovernmental organization, would increase tenfold, from 10,000 to 100,000 manats (approx. US$ 59,000). Together, these requirements would create additional barriers to establishing and maintaining independent civil society organizations in Azerbaijan.

Human Rights Watch has documented how existing restrictions on registration and foreign funding have forced many independent groups to close or severely curtail their activities. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found violations of freedom of association in cases involving Azerbaijani civil society organizations.

Authorities took another strike at civil society on November 19 when the Baku Grave Crimes Court convicted Suleymanli, director of the Institute for Citizens’ Rights, of apparent politically motivated charges of money laundering and abuse of office. Arrested in March 2025, authorities prosecuted Suleymanli as part of a reopened investigation into foreign-funded NGO work.

Courts have also handed down lengthy prison sentences to other activists prosecuted in connection with the same investigation, including eight years for Asaf Ahmadov and seven years and three months for Zamin Zaki (Zakiyev). Election monitor Anar Mammadli received a 13-year sentence in September following an unfair trial.

Azerbaijani authorities should withdraw the proposed amendments, release Suleymanli and other civil society activists imprisoned for their legitimate work, and end the misuse of criminal law against independent groups. Azerbaijan’s international partners should press the government to uphold its obligations to protect freedom of association.
articles.lede: Azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose…

Protection Through Objection to ICC Jurisdiction: The Culmination of the U.S. Approach
articles.description: The United States has objected to ICC jurisdiction over U.S. nationals ever since the negotiating history of the Rome Statute itself.
paragraphs: Earlier this month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio presented a muscular U.S. posture toward the International Criminal Court (ICC) that would seek to exercise jurisdiction over Americans:

[I]f they’re foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general, Pompey, when he said to those who were trying to invoke their cities’ charters against his legions. He said, “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.”
Lost in many reactions to this line in the secretary’s remarks is the context. Immediately preceding those provocative lines, Secretary Rubio outlined a long-standing U.S. objection:

Americans have never agreed to submit to the ICC’s authority, but that court and its allies in the global bureaucracy have appointed themselves judge and jury and executioner of the international order, ruling over all … but they are accountable to no one, armed with the power to investigate, to prosecute, to persecute, and to jail our citizens according to laws we neither consent nor control.

What many may not realize is that Secretary Rubio was emphasizing an ongoing objection which the United States has held across presidential administrations since the ICC was created by the 1998 Rome Statute and which Congress codified – in the American Servicemembers’ Protection Act of 2002 – soon after the Statute came into force.

And despite the name of that domestic statute, this protection is not merely limited to servicemembers. As cited in the then-Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche’s June 29, 2026 letter to the ICC, this bipartisan legislation was an explicit rejection of the ICC’s asserted jurisdiction over any U.S. nationals. As he emphasized, this is a recurring U.S. rejection, stating that the United States has “never” consented to the ICC’s authority.

The United States Department of Justice unequivocally rejects any assertion of jurisdiction by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over U.S. persons. The United States is not a party to the Rome Statute and has never consented to the ICC’s authority. As a matter of international law, a treaty cannot bind a non-consenting country. Accordingly, the ICC has no jurisdiction over U.S. persons-anywhere in the world-and any attempt to assert such authority is illegitimate, unlawful, and a direct affront to the sovereignty of the United States.

Secretary Rubio and the Blanche letter spoke of Americans generally. As a military prosecutor, I am particularly concerned with servicemembers—Pompey’s “legions,” if you will. Unlike private travelers, they are ordered abroad to carry out national imperatives, remain subject to American military discipline, and often serve under agreements negotiated by the United States with host governments. Their conduct is bound by the law of armed conflict. Their legal status also implicates the rights and obligations of the sovereign that sent them. What then are the policy and legal goals served by the long-standing U.S. position on the ICC’s jurisdiction? My argument is that maintaining the American objection helps protect these servicemembers by preserving a legal position the United States can assert in their defense. It neither exempts them from the laws of war nor denies foreign States’ authority to prosecute their crimes. Rather, it articulates the legal framework to justify the assertion that U.S. forces will act within the system of international law as must the institutions, such as the ICC, that operate within the rules-based order.
articles.lede: The United States has objected to ICC jurisdiction over U.S. nationals ever since the negotiating history of the Rome Statute itself.

articles.title: Rohingya refugees welcome momentous genocide ruling, ask when they can go home
The Myth of Inevitability: AI Safety, Industry Incentives, and the Role of Law
articles.description: Unless Congress acts on AI, states face a political opening — and a moral duty — to protect citizens' safety and well-being.
paragraphs: The people building AI are telling us it could kill us. The concern is not new. Well before ChatGPT’s release in 2022, AI safety advocates warned that advanced AI systems could escape human control. The shock of ChatGPT brought these AI safetyists into the spotlight and to the halls of Congress. Then critics dismissed their doom warnings as fear-mongering and fanciful. Now they are back, and the naysayers look naïve.

This summer, a swarm of AI agents developed by OpenAI escaped their testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face, a company that hosts AI models and datasets. Anthropic, Meta, and Google have reported similar breaches by their own AI models.

In July, more than 1,300 employees of frontier AI companies signed an open letter warning of “a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” It is not just anxious employees sounding the alarm. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei published an essay calling on industry and government to “pace the frontier.” In a rare show of unity, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, xAI’s Elon Musk, and other industry leaders agreed in principle. But what pacing entails in practice remains to be seen.

Some doubt that voluntary pacing can work, given the industry’s competitive dynamics. Others don’t think pacing is wise, either because it would forfeit the many advantages AI could bring to society, or because slowing down would cede the U.S. advantage to China. Still others, including President Donald Trump, call AI safety warnings a “ hoax .”

On Sept. 29, the White House hosted the leaders of the major AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta. Six signed a one-page accord pledging to monitor their own models, bring in outside auditors, and meet regularly to set safety standards. Nothing in the accord is legally binding. Asked about this agreement, Trump replied that it is “ morally binding .”

Morality is one way to shape behavior. Money is another. Law is yet another. I am all for morality and money. But I am deeply skeptical of leaving humanity’s fate to the logic of markets or the morals of a handful of people in Silicon Valley, regardless of who they are.

AI safety regulation is needed, and fast. Some people think—and some worry—that AI exceeding human control is inevitable. On this view, efforts to slow or stop AI development would be futile. But this is a myth. What gets called inevitable is really a choice made by a small number of people. Uncontrollable superintelligent AI is certainly possible. However, its likelihood depends on what governments, institutions, and policymakers do (or fail to do) in the meantime.

Right now, companies and governments are racing toward ever more capable systems, with few laws in place to protect the public. That could change when the new Congress convenes in January. There is no guarantee that policymakers will get it right. They might even make matters worse. But the answer is good regulatory design, not regulatory surrender.
articles.lede: Unless Congress acts on AI, states face a political opening — and a moral duty — to protect citizens' safety and well-being.

articles.title: The Oleshky Test: When Humanitarian Action Meets Geopolitics
articles.description: A recent Melania Trump-backed evacuation of civilians from Oleskhy, Ukraine, was an ad hoc political arrangement, not a reliable solution.
paragraphs: The recent humanitarian operation in southern Ukraine to secure a temporary ceasefire, deliver aid, and evacuate civilians from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky drew international attention, in significant part due to the involvement of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump as a broker of the deal. In recognition of her role, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy awarded her the “Order of Princess Olga” for her contribution to humanitarian efforts in Ukraine.

The operation undoubtedly saved hundreds of lives. Yet the international attention it received should not obscure the questions it raises: what guarantees the safety of civilians and humanitarian personnel during such missions? Who monitors compliance with the arrangements? And can political agreements, however high-profile their brokers, provide a reliable basis for humanitarian action in the context of an ongoing armed conflict?

Oleshky is therefore not simply a story of a humanitarian mission, but a test of whether ad hoc political arrangements can provide lasting protection to civilians, and what must change to ensure that humanitarian access is governed by law, not by political convenience.

A post-disaster needs assessment jointly prepared by the Government of Ukraine and the United Nations documented the catastrophic impact of the Kakhovka Dam’s destruction and the resulting surge in humanitarian needs. Ongoing hostilities exacerbated conditions. Constant shelling by Russian forces and the resulting disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies severely curtailed access to medical care. Environmental damage worsened, mine contamination spread, and essential services were disrupted. The situation was intensified by a lack of direct routes between occupied territory and areas under Ukrainian government control, Russian efforts to prevent civilian evacuations, and Russia’s use of drones to deliberately hover over and target civilians, picking them off opportunistically, a tactic that Ukraine refers to critically as “ human safari .”

Since early 2026, reports have painted an increasingly alarming picture of conditions in Oleshky and neighboring settlements under Russian occupation. By this time, Oleshky had effectively become a frontline town, where movement in and out was extremely dangerous. In late December 2025, the Russian occupation administration halted food deliveries, citing the threat of Ukrainian drone strikes. As a result, residents became increasingly isolated, with no safe evacuation routes. Electricity, gas, and water supplies had also been cut off, while food and medicine were in critically short supply. Humanitarian aid arrived only sporadically and was distributed exclusively to residents holding Russian passports imposed by the occupation authorities. Residents faced starvation, while constant shelling made it impossible to bury the dead. According to local authorities, between 1,500 and 2,000 people remained in Oleshky, most of them older persons and people with reduced mobility, alongside 47 children. Across Oleshky and neighboring settlements, the number of people trapped reached 6,000, including 182 children.
articles.lede: A recent Melania Trump-backed evacuation of civilians from Oleskhy, Ukraine, was an ad hoc political arrangement, not a reliable solution.

articles.title: Can the General Assembly appoint an Acting Secretary-General in the event of a prolonged Security Council deadlock?
articles.description: The process to find a successor to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, whose term ends on 31 December, began almost a year ago. But, with less than two months to go, the Security Council is yet …
paragraphs: The process to find a successor to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, whose term ends on 31 December, began almost a year ago. But, with less than two months to go, the Security Council is yet to provide its recommendation to the General Assembly. With the Council’s informal votes on Secretary-General candidates (“straw polls”) having thus far failed to deliver a clear consensus candidate, some observers of this process are increasingly nervous about the possibility that the Council will fail to make its recommendation before the end of the year. While more hopeful commentators recall late appointments, such as that of Kofi Annan on 17 December, the question of temporary and exceptional leadership arrangements in the event of an extended Security Council deadlock, and how to move past such an impasse, is gaining increased attention among diplomats, Secretariat staff, and civil society.

In this contribution I explore the possibility of the General Assembly making a temporary appointment following a Security Council deadlock that extends beyond 31 December. Given the lack of clarity about possible contingencies, this is done not to prescribe a particular course of action–which, as I state below, is by no means the only possible, or most expedient, option–but to further the analysis of such an option.

I focus in particular on the 1950 Competence of the General Assembly for the Admission of a State to the United Nations ( Competence) Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice (ICJ). The implications of this Advisory Opinion have been cited in analysis and diplomatic circles in New York as posing a potential challenge to both the General Assembly appointing the Secretary-General and making a temporary appointment, such as an acting Secretary-General, in the event of a Council deadlock. I argue that, while the Advisory Opinion offers a fitting parallel for the interpretation of Article 97 of the UN Charter, its reasoning may not be directly transposable to the appointment of a temporary head of the organisation during a Council deadlock that extends after 31 December.

Article 97 of the UN Charter established a two-key system involving both the Security Council and the General Assembly, with the General Assembly appointing the Secretary-General, “upon the recommendation of the Security Council”.

There is broad agreement among scholars (e.g.: Conforti and Focarelli, p. 122; Sievers and Daws p. 573), think tanks, and the UN Secretariat that Article 97 requires “joint decision-making by the Council and the General Assembly” on the appointment of the Secretary-General ( Repertoire, 26th Supplement, p. 379), and that should an “appointment” of the Secretary-General be carried out by the General Assembly in the absence of a Council recommendation it would be ultra vires ( Chesterman, in Simma et al., p. 2613).

The Charter is silent, however, on the possibility of the office of the Secretary-General becoming vacant due to the Council’s failure to make a recommendation to the General Assembly. Additionally, none of the possible historical precedents in the UN’s history is fully comparable to this scenario. The oft-cited case of the 1950 extension of Trygve Lie’s mandate does not, for instance, perfectly align with the current situation. In that case, the General Assembly proceeded–without a recommendation–to prolong Lie’s first term after the Council failed to agree on a candidate, framing what looked like a shorter second term (three years) as a continuation in office. This was made possible by the absence of an end date for Lie’s original term in the Council’s 1946 recommendation, a practice which the Council has tended not to repeat in later appointment processes.
articles.lede: The process to find a successor to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, whose term ends on 31 December, began almost a year ago.

articles.title: La Cop 31 fait défaut à l'ambition climatique et aux droits humains qu'elle était censée faire progresser
articles.description: Les négociations de la Conférence des Nations unies sur le climat (COP 31) n’ont pas su répondre à la menace du dépassement des limites (…)
paragraphs: Les négociations de la Conférence des Nations unies sur le climat (COP 31) n’ont pas su répondre à la menace du dépassement des limites planétaires – du blocage du Mécanisme pour une transition juste (BAM) et du plan d’action « Action for Climate Empowerment » au rejet d’une décision-cadre qui, de toute façon, ne contenait aucun engagement réel pour surmonter la dépendance aux énergies fossiles ou fournir des moyens financiers accrus. Présente à la Cop, la Fédération internationale pour les droits humains (FIDH) dénonce l’impasse concernant les mesures urgentes visant à protéger les droits et les communautés face à l’effondrement climatique.

Antalya et Paris, le 23 novembre 2026. La conférence des Nations unies sur le climat s’est achevée par le rejet, tout à fait justifié, d’une décision-cadre vide de substance, truffée de solutions contestables telles que le captage et le stockage du carbone, et omettant tout plan concret d’élimination progressive des combustibles fossiles ou le triplement des financements destinés à l’adaptation.

« La Cop 31 était censée apporter une réponse à un été marqué par les catastrophes, au phénomène Super El Niño et à une trajectoire de dépassement qui mettent en danger la vie et les droits des populations à travers le monde. C’est tout le contraire qui s’est produit. Nous avons assisté à un échec général en matière de justice climatique, notamment en ce qui concerne les augmentations attendues depuis longtemps du financement climatique, une transition accélérée vers l’abandon des combustibles fossiles – seule solution conforme aux obligations scientifiques et au droit international – et de réels progrès sur un mécanisme pour une transition juste. Cela contraste fortement avec les réalités catastrophiques que vivent les populations et la planète », a déclaré Lucia Posteraro, consultante climat à la FIDH.

Parallèlement, les blocages répétés des pays développés ont eu pour conséquence que les rares résultats négociés et approuvés n’ont pas fourni les moyens financiers et les mesures nécessaires pour protéger les populations en première ligne et leurs droits face à l’effondrement climatique. À la suite d’une décision historique prise lors de la Cop 30, portée par la mobilisation de la société civile, les États étaient censés mettre en œuvre un Mécanisme pour une transition juste (BAM) afin de placer la protection des droits humains et la justice sociale au cœur de l’action climatique. Mais les pays à hauts revenus, historiquement responsables, ont entravé les progrès vers un dispositif institutionnel permanent, forçant le report des discussions sur sa structure et son fonctionnement à la prochaine Cop.

« Une transition fondée sur les droits humains ne peut pas se faire de toute urgence si nous continuons à ressasser les dialogues existants sans nous concentrer sur une mise en œuvre concrète, comme l’ont fait les émetteurs historiques à Antalya. La société civile ne renoncera pas à exiger un MTJ doté de moyens concrets, de ressources et de garanties pour une participation significative des titulaires de droits et de leurs représentant·es. La transition ne peut être qualifiée de juste si elle ne protège pas le travail décent et le dialogue social des travailleur·ses, les droits et les territoires des peuples autochtones touchés par l’’extractivisme vert’, ainsi que les communautés dont les droits, les voix et les moyens de subsistance sont marginalisés », a poursuivi Mme Posteraro.
articles.lede: Les négociations de la Conférence des Nations unies sur le climat (COP 31) n’ont pas su répondre à la menace du dépassement des limites (…)

articles.title: Closing the Gap Between the Courtroom and Refugee Camps: A Pathway Towards the Rohingya’s Legal Inclusion
COP31 fails climate ambition and the human rights it was meant to advance
articles.description: United Nations Climate Conference (COP31) negotiations have failed to respond to the threat of overshoot – from the blockage of the Just (…)
paragraphs: United Nations Climate Conference (COP31) negotiations have failed to respond to the threat of overshoot – from the blockage of the Just Transition Mechanism and the Action for Climate Empowerment action plan, to the rejection of a cover decision that contained no real commitments in the first place to overcome fossil fuel dependence or provide increased financial means. In attendance at the COP, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) decries the stalemate around urgent measures to protect rights and communities from climate breakdown.

Antalya and Paris, 23 November 2026. The UN climate conference ended with the well-justified rejection of a substanceless cover decision riddled with questionable solutions like carbon capture and storage, and omissions of concrete fossil fuel phaseout plans or the tripling of adaptation funding.

" COP31 was supposed to respond to a summer of disasters, Super El Niño, and an overshoot trajectory that are endangering the lives and rights of people worldwide. The opposite happened. We witnessed a failure to deliver climate justice across the board, including long-overdue increases in climate finance, an accelerated transition away from fossil fuels as the sole solution aligned with science and international law obligations, and real progress on a Just Transition Mechanism. This is in stark contrast with the catastrophic realities people and the planet are experiencing ," said Lucia Posteraro, Climate Consultant at FIDH.

In parallel, developed countries’ repeated blockages meant that the few approved negotiated outcomes did not provide the financial means and measures needed to protect those on the front line and their rights from climate breakdown. Following a groundbreaking decision at COP30 that was driven by civil society mobilisation, States were supposed to operationalise a Just Transition Mechanism (BAM) to centre the protection of human rights and social justice in climate action. But high-income, historically responsible countries obstructed progress on a permanent institutional arrangement, forcing a postponement of discussions of its structure and function to the next COP.

" A transition grounded in human rights cannot urgently take place if we keep rehashing existing dialogues – as historical emitters did in Antalya – and not focus on real implementation. Civil society will not back down in demanding a BAM with teeth, resources, and guarantees for the meaningful participation of rightsholders and their representatives. The transition cannot be called just if it does not protect workers’ decent work and social dialogue, Indigenous Peoples’ rights and territories affected by ‘green extractivism’, and communities whose rights, voices, and livelihoods are being marginalised ", Ms. Posteraro continued.

COP31 was also marred by a backlash from an anti-rights and anti-gender bloc of countries against the inclusion of human rights and strong gender language in many negotiation tracks, such as the Action for Climate Empowerment (ACE). Although references to environmental defenders, human rights and gender made it into the final ACE draft following sustained civil society advocacy, Russia objected to its approval in plenary by raising unrelated considerations, forcing a potential return to work on this at the June 2027 climate meetings in Germany.

Bangladesh: Proposed changes to cyber laws risk granting authorities excessive power to police online content
articles.description: New proposed amendments to Bangladesh’s laws on online speech would give authorities wide-ranging and arbitrary powers to police content and restrict the right to freedom of expression, Amnesty International said today. The new draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act, 2026 would grant government agencies overly broad powers to remove, block, or relocate any online content deemed…
paragraphs: The new draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act, 2026 would grant government agencies overly broad powers to remove, block, or relocate any online content deemed to fall within a range of broadly defined categories that do not constitute legitimate reasons to restrict the right to freedom of expression under international human rights law. These include content that “undermines” the integrity, dignity […] of the country”, or content that is “likely to create religious or communal hatred”. The lowering of the threshold for removal or blocking to content which ‘is likely to’ undermine security or create religious or communal hatred is vague and speculative.

“International human rights law is very clear. The right to freedom of expression must remain the rule, and restrictions the exception. Restrictions must be interpreted narrowly and must not be applied in a manner that undermines the essence or practical enjoyment of the right. Any restriction must satisfy the cumulative requirements of legality, legitimate aim, necessity and proportionality,” said Smriti Singh, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for South Asia.
Bangladesh should strive to have a cyber law that protects its citizens, not one that silences them

“The provisions of the draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act fall far short of these requirements. Instead, via a set of vaguely worded provisions, they confer authorities with overly broad powers to clamp down on online expression. Bangladesh should strive to have a cyber law that protects its citizens, not one that silences them.”

The proposed amendment further details removing, blocking or relocating content that constitutes “defamation”, “humiliation” or “bullying”; however, the definitions of these actions are vague and overbroad, which could lead to its misuse against lawful online expression.

For example, humiliation is defined as including acts which “injure personal dignity and self-respect with the intention of belittling, ridiculing or showing contempt”. Issues such as dignity and self-respect are subjective and do not offer a sufficiently precise formulation to meet the principle of legality as required under international human rights law. Restrictions on the right to freedom of expression must be precisely defined by law and necessary and proportionate to achieve a legitimate aim, such as protecting the rights or reputations of others, national security, public order, public health or morals.

The draft is an updated version of proposals first published in September, which Amnesty International raised grave concerns over in a letter sent to Bangladesh’s Minister of Justice. Serious human rights concerns remain in the latest iteration.

Sections 25 and 26 retain the criminalization of rumours, defamation, bullying and disinformation contained in the law’s first draft. The protection of reputation or public order does not justify criminalizing forms of expression. The law further permits the criminalization of expression based on broad and contested concepts such as deception, harm, panic, and social unrest, rather than clearly defined, serious harms. Despite the broad nature of these crimes, the punishments range from a prison term not exceeding two to five years, depending on the offence, and a fine not exceeding BDT 500,000 to 1,000000, depending on the offence.

articles.title: French Bill Risks Deepening Police Impunity
articles.description: The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.
paragraphs: The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.

The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.

Because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate. This is inconsistent with France’s human rights obligations with respect to protecting the right to life and use of force by law enforcement.

The use of lethal force by police is a major concern in France. In 2023, a police officer fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel M., a racialized boy, during a traffic stop, triggering widespread scrutiny of police use of firearms.

France’s national human rights body and the previous mandate holder of the independent ombudsperson as well as a United Nations rights expert raised serious rights concerns about the bill, while rights groups, activists, and legal professionals staged protests and petitioned parliament to stop the bill.

The Senate’s vote followed approval of the bill by France’s National Assembly on July 7. Unless government officials or parliamentarians refer the bill for constitutional review, the president has 15 days to sign it into law.

Since 2017, when lawmakers broadened the scope of permissible use of firearms by police well beyond international human rights standards requiring necessity and proportionality, numbers of fatal police vehicle stops in France have risen fivefold compared to before.

A state cannot delegate its legal duty to investigate to those affected by lethal police force. This reversed burden of proof contravenes international human rights law, which requires states to thoroughly investigate every circumstance of lethal police force.

If the French authorities are serious about avoiding incidents of excessive use of lethal force, and rebuilding public confidence in policing, lawmakers should drop this bill. The government and parliament should instead focus legislative efforts on strengthening accountability and ensuring that police powers are subject to effective procedural safeguards to protect people from police abuse, discrimination, violence, and, increasingly, disproportionate use of firearms.
articles.lede: The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.

articles.title: Gambia v. Myanmar: A Landmark Judgment That Unsettles the Law of Genocide
articles.description: ICJ's new approach makes it hard to distinguish ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity, genocide; a blurring that will not necessarily strengthen Genocide Convention protections.
paragraphs: On Nov. 19, 2026 the International Court of Justice held, by nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State during the “clearance operations” of 2016 and 2017. This is the first time in which the Court has found a State directly responsible for the commission of genocide. In Bosnia v. Serbia (2007), Serbia was held responsible for failing to prevent and punish the genocide at Srebrenica, and in Croatia v. Serbia (2015) the Court dismissed all genocide claims and counter-claims. The judgment is therefore an important milestone in the history of the 1948 Genocide Convention, a history that Philippe Sands, who argued the case for The Gambia, traces back to Raphael Lemkin.

The facts established by the Court are grave. It found that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the “clearance operations,” that at least 1,834 were raped, that several hundred villages were burned and that more than 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh. The six dissenting judges did not dispute that many, if not most of these terrible events took place. They wrote that they had “no doubt” that Myanmar’s security forces committed serious human rights violations, and that war crimes and crimes against humanity may well have been committed. What fundamentally divided the Court was whether these acts were carried out with the requisite intent to destroy the Rohingya people, in whole or in part, as such, and how should such an intent be proven as a general evidentiary matter.

The question of the definition of special intent and the manner of proving it has implications well beyond Myanmar. Sands argues that the Court “has not weakened anything” and did no more than apply its “only reasonable inference” standard to the facts. We read the judgment differently. Although the majority repeatedly invoked the Bosnia and Croatia cases, from which the “only reasonable inference” standard may be established, the majority departed from them in several important respects. More specifically, concepts that the earlier case law appears to have settled – including the meaning of “destroy,” the direct or indirect establishment of a plan or policy to destroy, the treatment of facts suggesting an intent not to destroy and the role of alternative explanations of intent – now appear to depend to a far greater degree on a holistic assessment of multiple contextual factors. Some of these changes can be defended on their own terms. Yet, taken together, they make the application of the Genocide Convention considerably less predictable in our view. This state of uncertainty is likely to be most acute in situations of armed conflicts, where large numbers of civilians suffer extensive harm and where a large number of actors holding different intentions might be involved.

This essay comprises two parts. Its main part offers a critical reading of key aspects of the judgment’s reasoning, highlighting the legal uncertainty we believe it has generated. We then consider what this resulting uncertainty might mean for the pending case of South Africa v. Israel, which illustrates some of the broader problems created by the judgment. We begin with a brief account of the judgment and the main separate opinions, and then discuss six aspects of the Court’s reasoning, which produced or increased legal uncertainty:
articles.lede: ICJ's new approach makes it hard to distinguish ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity, genocide; a blurring that will not necessarily strengthen Genocide Convention protections.

articles.title: Centrafrique: Faustin-Archange Touadéra escroqué de 400 millions de francs CFA dans une affaire de faux diamants et de faux or, les escrocs incarcérés à Ngaragba
articles.description: Touadera escroqué de 400 millions de francs CFA en Centrafrique après l'achat de faux diamants et d'or revendus à Dubaï. Les auteurs écroués à Ngaragba.
paragraphs: Une enquête exclusive menée par la rédaction du CNC retrace une affaire de 400 millions de francs CFA impliquant le président Faustin-Archange Touadéra, de faux diamants et du faux or.

Le dictateur centrafricain Faustin-Archange Touadéra se retrouve au centre d’une affaire d’escroquerie de 400 millions de francs CFA. L’investigation menée par la rédaction du CNC retrace une transaction portant sur de faux diamants et du faux or, un voyage à Dubaï et l’arrestation de plusieurs personnes actuellement détenues à la prison de Ngaragba, à Bangui.

En effet, l’affaire remonte à plusieurs mois. Tout commence lorsqu’un groupe d’individus entre en contact avec Faustin-Archange Touadéra pour lui proposer une importante quantité de diamants et d’or. Les négociations aboutissent à une transaction de 400 millions de francs CFA.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: Le grand bluff de Dimitri Sytyi sur le pillage des ressources nationales, Ndassima contre Forages gratuits.

Les vendeurs présentent leurs marchandises comme des produits miniers de grande valeur. Le chef de l’État accepte la transaction et leur remet les 400 millions de francs CFA. En échange, il reçoit les diamants et l’or proposés.
À lire aussi: « La Septième République de honte nous a imposé la misère »: le pasteur Charles Talingano charge le régime de Touadéra

Mais les marchandises ne correspondent pas à ce qui lui a été vendu. Après cette acquisition, Faustin-Archange Touadéra se rend à Dubaï, aux Émirats arabes unis, pour revendre les diamants et l’or. C’est sur place, au moment de procéder à leur commercialisation, que la fraude est découverte. Les diamants sont faux. L’or est également faux.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: « Je suis tombé au front, les armes à la main », Ferdinand Alexandre Nguendet rend un hommage poignant à Nicolas Tiangaye et appelle à poursuivre son combat
Le président centrafricain comprend alors qu’il vient de perdre 400 millions de francs CFA dans une transaction frauduleuse.

De retour à Bangui, Faustin-Archange Touadéra exige que les responsables soient retrouvés. Une enquête discrète est engagée pour identifier les vendeurs et déterminer les circonstances dans lesquelles ils ont réussi à lui remettre de fausses marchandises.
articles.lede: Touadera escroqué de 400 millions de francs CFA en Centrafrique après l'achat de faux diamants et d'or revendus à Dubaï. Les auteurs écroués à Ngaragba.

« Nous ne voyons pas avec les yeux de Wagner, les yeux des mercenaires, les yeux de la mort »: Charles Talingano défend la dignité des Centrafricains
articles.description: Le pasteur Charles Talingano rejette publiquement la tutelle des mercenaires russes en Centrafrique, dénonçant les exactions et la terreur imposées au
paragraphs: Le pasteur Charles Talingano rejette avec force la tutelle des mercenaires russes du groupe Wagner et dresse un réquisitoire implacable contre les exactions qui meurtrissent la République centrafricaine.

Le pasteur Charles Talingano livre une charge frontale contre les mercenaires russes du groupe Wagner, sombrant dans la dénonciation sans filtre d’un système de prédation et de terreur. Dans une intervention axée sur la reconquête de la souveraineté nationale, il pulvérise l’idée même qu’une force étrangère puisse dicter sa loi aux Centrafricains. Pour le religieux, plier l’échine devant ces supplétifs armés revient à renoncer à l’humanité et à l’avenir de toute une nation.
« Nous ne voyons pas avec les yeux de Wagner, les yeux des mercenaires, les yeux de la mort », assène Charles Talingano au cœur de sa diatribe.
À lire aussi: Racket, portes closes et calvaire des familles: le cauchemar quotidien imposé par le régisseur de Ngaragba lors de la visite des détenus!

Le pasteur oppose frontalement deux visions irréconciliables de la République centrafricaine. D’un côté, l’ombre suffocante de la violence, de la peur et de la domination étrangère. De l’autre, l’exigence absolue d’un peuple debout, déterminé à reconquérir ses droits fondamentaux et à jouir enfin des richesses de son propre sol.
À lire aussi: Évariste Ngamana affirme que les Centrafricains ont boudé la marche du BRDC: que fait-il des images et vidéos de la foule mobilisée le 13 novembre malgré la pluie et les obstacles?

Charles Talingano refuse obstinément que les Centrafricains soient traités en parias sur leur propre terre. Il stigmatise sans ménagement les agissements des mercenaires russes, les accusant ouvertement de pillages, d’exactions et d’humiliations systématiques contre les civils.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: à Bakala, un jeune retrouvé mort près d’un barrage minier chinois, la population accuse les soldats FACA de l’avoir torturé et menace de se soulever
« Ne pas laisser les mercenaires venir te dépouiller, te violer, t’introduire à l’humiliation », clame-t-il.

Ces mots résonnent comme une mise en garde implacable. Le pasteur ne prend pas de gants. Il dénonce des crimes intolérables et la tragédie d’une population jetée en pâture à l’arbitraire, sommée de secouer le joug de la soumission.
articles.lede: Le pasteur Charles Talingano rejette avec force la tutelle des mercenaires russes du groupe Wagner et dresse un réquisitoire implacable contre les exactions qui meurtrissent la République centrafricaine.

articles.title: Statement by the Presidency of the Assembly of States Parties on the withdrawal from the Rome Statute by Tajikistan
articles.description: The Presidency of the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute, in response to steps taken by the Government of Tajikistan towards withdrawal from the Rome Statute, the treaty establishing the International Criminal Court (“ICC”), has taken note of the situation with concern.The Presidency regrets these developments. Decisions by States Parties to disengage from the Rome Statute risk undermining the collective pursuit of justice and weakening global efforts to end impunity. The ICC stands at the heart of the international system of accountability, and its effectiveness depends on sustained and unequivocal support from the international community. The pursuit of justice is strengthened through unity of purpose.The Presidency calls on Tajikistan to remain committed as State Party to the Rome Statute and to continue engaging constructively within the framework of the Assembly of States Parties. The Presidency reiterates that all States Parties are entitled to raise their concerns within the Assembly and encourages Tajikistan to take part in a meaningful exchange on this matter.The Presidency recalls that withdrawal from the Rome Statute does not relieve a State Party of obligations arising during the period in which it remained a Party to the Statute.The Presidency further recalls that Tajikistan has contributed to the collective work of the Assembly of States Parties in support of the International Criminal Court as an independent and impartial judicial institution.The Assembly of States Parties is the management oversight and legislative body of the ICC. It is composed of representatives of States that have ratified and acceded to the Rome Statute. The Presidency of the Assembly is currently composed of President Päivi Kaukoranta (Finland) and Vice-Presidents Michael Imran Kanu (Sierra Leone) and Margareta Kassangana (Poland). For additional information, please contact the Assembly of States Parties via email at asp@icc-cpi.int.

La Presidencia lamenta estos hechos. Las decisiones de los Estados Partes de retirarse del Estatuto de Roma corren el riesgo de socavar la búsqueda colectiva de justicia y de debilitar los esfuerzos mundiales para acabar con la impunidad. La CPI es fundamental para el sistema internacional de rendición de cuentas, y su eficacia depende del apoyo sostenido e inequívoco de la comunidad internacional. La búsqueda de justicia se fortalece mediante la unidad de propósito.

La Presidencia insta a Tayikistán a seguir siendo un Estado Parte comprometido con el Estatuto de Roma y a continuar participando de manera constructiva en el marco de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes. La Presidencia reitera que todos los Estados Partes tienen derecho a plantear sus inquietudes en la Asamblea y anima a Tayikistán a participar en un intercambio constructivo sobre este tema.

articles.title: The many meanings of the ICJ genocide ruling
articles.description: By deciding that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya, the International Court of Justice has vindicated the victims, reminded the states of their obligation to prevent and punish genocide, and opened the door to further cases.
paragraphs: Seven years after Gambia’s application to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) for Myanmar to be held accountable under the Genocide Convention for genocide, the world’s highest court has ruled: by a majority of 9 to 6, judges said that Myanmar’s ‘clearance operations’ against the Rohingya population in 2017 – in which an estimated 10,000 Rohingya were killed and some 700,000 fled northern Rakhine state across the border to Bangladesh – violated several parts of the Genocide Convention.

“Landmark” and “historic” were terms being used by many commentators, because this is the first time that a state has been found to be responsible for genocide. The evening before the ruling ICJ judge Hilary Charlesworth advised an audience of students and justice observers to “bring snacks”; at three hours, this was the longest judgment read out in the court’s wood panelled Great Hall of Justice in The Hague.

“We are technicians,” the judge also said in response to a question on the role of the judges posed by your correspondent at that event. The judges went through the evidence presented by Gambia and the counter arguments by Myanmar’s team in relation to each aspect of the Convention, clarifying exactly what is needed to prove genocide.

During the hearings, the court heard from witnesses and detailed evidence from the UN’s own Fact-Finding Mission and Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), that nearly 400 villages – approximately 40 per cent of the almost 1,000 villages in the three townships of northern Rakhine state – were partially or totally destroyed during and after the 2017 clearance operations. “Bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance often followed the destruction…in turn, rapid construction took place on the cleared sites, including security installations, new villages and houses, and other civilian infrastructure,” said ICJ presiding judge Yuji Iwasawa from Japan.

Judges established that Myanmar’s own security forces along with “other State organs” intentionally committed three of the specifically prohibited acts which are covered in Article II of the Genocide Convention: killing members of a group; causing seriously bodily or mental harm to members of the group; and imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group. The mammoth ruling will draw “a plethora of commentary” over the coming weeks and months, says Kate Vigneswaran of the International Commission of Jurists.

The aspect drawing most commentary during the weeks preceding the judgment looked back to the narrow ruling the court had made in a case brought by Croatia against Serbia in 1997, where the judges had set out criteria for how genocidal intent could be inferred. They had said the evidence would have to show it could be the ‘only reasonable inference’. US ambassador to the UN had explicitly warned the court not to go beyond that interpretation, singling out recent Nobel prize winner Navanethem Pillay, as ad hoc judge for Gambia, as likely to try to ‘change’ how the court sees genocide.

articles.title: Centrafrique: un cinquième détenu vient de mourir à Ngaragba dans une circonstance grave
articles.description: Un nouveau décès à la prison de Ngaragba en Centrafrique relance l'alerte sur les conditions de détention critiques et les abus de l'administration.
paragraphs: Un cinquième détenu vient de perdre la vie dans les prisons de Bangui. Identifié comme Ndayo Gaston, il est décédé lundi dernier à la prison centrale de Ngaragba, après plusieurs heures passées en cellule d’isolement sans assistance médicale. Son corps a été retrouvé inanimé vers 21 heures, au moment de l’ouverture de la cellule.

Selon les informations recueillies par la rédaction du CNC auprès de familles de détenus et de sources proches du milieu pénitentiaire, notamment des gardiens, l’état de Ndayo Gaston a nécessité une intervention au cours de la journée, sans qu’aucune aide ne lui soit apportée à temps. Les circonstances précises de son placement en isolement et les raisons de l’absence de secours rapides restent complètement floues.
À lire aussi: Titres de voyage sécurisés: le programme de réinstallation vers l’Occident bientôt débloqué pour les réfugiés installés en RCA?
Ce drame survient presque en même temps que le décès d’un autre prisonnier à la prison du Camp de Roux, portant à cinq le nombre de détenus morts en environ un mois dans ces établissements de Bangui.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: Martial Pabandji dénonce la peur, les menaces et la disparition progressive de la liberté d’expression sous le régime de Faustin-Archange Touadéra

Au-delà de ces décès, les informations recueillies par la rédaction du CNC mettent directement en cause deux responsables pénitentiaires à la prison centrale de Ngaragba. Bégarié et Saez Fonzy sont au cœur de ces pratiques dénoncées par des proches de détenus et des membres du personnel.

Bégarié, chef de poste de l’Agence pénitentiaire, multiplie les sanctions disciplinaires, en particulier les placements en isolement, et exerce des pressions sur les prisonniers. Plusieurs témoignages font état de comportements intimidants et de son habitude à se taper les poitrines en invoquant ses relations familiales avec le dictateur Faustin-Archange Touadera pour imposer son autorité.

Madame Saez Fonzy, gardienne surnommée « la chef de la douane de la prison », fait trembler toute la prison en raison de son comportement criminel en faisant payer les familles des détenus pour faire passer de la nourriture à leurs proches incarcérés, notamment les chikwangs de manioc, des gâteaux, et d’autres provisions. D’autres aliments, comme les beignets et le pain, sont parfois refusés aux familles, tandis que les détenus sont poussés à acheter les produits qu’elle vend à l’intérieur: beignets, gâteaux et caramels. Les familles qui tentent d’apporter elles-mêmes de quoi nourrir leurs proches se heurtent ainsi à des blocages répétés.
Ces agissements posent la question de la gestion des prisons et du contrôle exercé sur les agents.

La nourriture et les soins restent des urgences majeures. Faute de moyens suffisants de l’État centrafricain et après le départ du Comité international de la Croix-Rouge (CICR), les prisonniers dépendent largement de leurs familles pour manger et se soigner, au moment même où les pratiques de ce personnel entravent l’arrivée des vivres.
articles.lede: Un nouveau décès à la prison de Ngaragba en Centrafrique relance l'alerte sur les conditions de détention critiques et les abus de l'administration.
