articles.title: Regulating ‘Killer Robots’: another missed opportunity?
articles.description: On 16-20 November in Geneva States will deliberate on what could form the basis of a future Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) instrument. But what does this mean for civilian protection and meeting the challenges of algorithmic warfare?
paragraphs: One glance at recent headlines on automated and accelerated decision-making in targeting in Gaza, Iran, Ukraine and elsewhere, shows how far the time required for doubt, reflection – and human witnessing – has been stripped, without a corresponding emphasis on understanding and accounting for what is lost for civilians forced to exist and survive in these conflicts.

Over the past two decades, artificial intelligence (AI) in the military domain, which includes a reliance on algorithmic decision-support systems and predictive pattern-of-life targeting, has dramatically altered how war is experienced, and how crucial parts of International Humanitarian Law (IHL) – such as civilian status – are interpreted.

In early September 2026, the final meeting of the United Nations group of governmental experts (GGE) on emerging technologies in the area of Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems concluded a final text of “elements for an instrument”, adopted by states, available to read online. The text will be presented to delegations convening in Geneva, the Swiss capital of diplomacy, at the seventh review conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons – commonly referred to as the ‘CCW’ – which will be held this month from 16 to 20th November 2026.

A reading of the text – often referred to as “regulating killer robots” – generates a disturbing disconnect from the reality of today’s wars and raises questions about whether a treaty in this forum could ever serve to restrain autonomous or artificial intelligence-assisted uses of force.

The 1980 CCW is an international treaty banning or restricting the use of weapons considered to cause unnecessary or unjustifiable suffering to combatants and indiscriminate harm to civilians, in both international and non-international armed conflicts. It operates through five annexed protocols, designed to be added to, which address specific categories of harmful weapons:

Could there be a sixth protocol on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (also known by the acronym LAWS)? Possibly. The CCW was designed to be a flexible convention, so new weapons protocols could be added to it over time. Under article 8 of the CCW, any state that has ratified the treaty has the power to propose an additional protocol relating to categories of conventional weapons not yet covered, and a conference to negotiate a protocol can proceed if a majority of states agree. Or, states can collectively decide on new protocol negotiations at a meeting.

Because the CCW operates by consensus, a decision can only be made if no member state actively objects to it. This enables broad participation on the one hand, but on the other hand means that the CCW requires the passive or explicit agreement of every single participating state, which has implications for how text is negotiated – vetoed and blocked, or compromised and diluted. Some states embrace consensus and others instrumentalise it, diluting the collective will and ambition, as Yvette Issar from the Quaker UN Office in Geneva, has reflected on.
articles.lede: On 16-20 November in Geneva States will deliberate on what could form the basis of a future Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) instrument.

articles.title: 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Ownership of a Style – Ghibli-Style Generation and the Limits of Copyright within the Territorial Framework
articles.description: [Lakshmidevi Somanath is Partner – Litigation & Strategy at Anand and Anand, India and a PhD Scholar at IIT Kharagpur. She formerly served in the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, Go…
paragraphs: [ Lakshmidevi Somanath is Partner – Litigation & Strategy at Anand and Anand, India and a PhD Scholar at IIT Kharagpur. She formerly served in the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, Government of India as a Member Judge.]

In March 2025, the launch of native image generation together with GPT-4o created an avalanche of family photos and movie posters recreated in the unique soft hand-painted style that is specific for Studio Ghibli. The explanation given by the provider defined the line separating persons and organizations, with the model being capable of rejecting a prompt referring to a living artist but accepting those associated with more general studio styles. On the contrary, the copyright law makes no such distinction, and reactions from practicing artists confirmed this fact.

Eighteen months on, the question has moved from the timeline to the docket. In October 2025 the Content Overseas Distribution Association, whose members include Studio Ghibli, asked OpenAI to stop using members’ works for machine learning and to answer infringement claims arising from Sora 2 outputs, and the Japanese Cabinet Office made a formal request of its own. In November, the Regional Court of Munich I held that song lyrics memorised in model parameters, and reproduced in chatbot outputs, infringed German copyright.

The case provides a genuine test for three propositions put forward by clients during a single counseling session, namely: (1) style is unprotectable, (2) training is subject to the laws of the particular jurisdiction in which it occurs, and (3) moral rights arise where economic rights are inadequate. All three propositions hold true, at least in part.

First of all, this postulate is well-established and universally accepted. According to TRIPS Article 9(2), copyright covers expression rather than an idea, procedure, or method of operation. Similarly, the Berne Convention only covers the works of literary and artistic nature rather than the manner of their creation. Palette, line weight, weather depiction, and pacing of a cut belong to the latter category and are therefore not protected under Berne Convention.

This position is corroborated in all jurisdictions involved. Japan’s General Understanding on AI and Copyright published by the Cultural Council’s Legal Subcommittee in March 2024 considers the act of infringement at the output stage as involving two elements – resemblance to the concrete expression of a copyrighted work and reliance on the expression. The former is usually presumed if the work in question is included into the training data (as per Tatsuhiro Ueno, who is a member of the subcommittee). Simply being similar to the manner of expression is not enough. In the same fashion, the US Copyright Office has reached this doctrinal conclusion in Part 3 of the report on generative AI training, albeit with some shift in focus – the concept of stylistic substitution is considered as market harm under the fourth factor of fair use doctrine.

The practical consequence is that liability is assessed output by output rather than trend by trend. The forensic question is whether the image is in the style of the catalogue or of a work within it, and the answer rarely turns on the wording of the prompt. Copyright attaches to works and to the rights subsisting in them, and is indifferent to whether an aesthetic is attributable to one director or to several hundred animators.
articles.lede: In March 2025, the launch of native image generation together with GPT-4o created an avalanche of family photos and movie posters recreated in the unique soft hand-painted style that is specific for Studio Ghibli.

articles.title: A collective step forward: the outcome document on achieving meaningful protection for hospitals in armed conflict
cats: Upholding humanity in war: the Global IHL Initiative
articles.description: When war reaches hospitals, protection becomes a matter of life and death. Discover what international humanitarian law demands.
paragraphs: Hospitals and other medical facilities enjoy specific protection under international humanitarian law (IHL), yet the reality in contemporary armed conflicts is starkly different. Attacks against health-care facilities, their misuse and impediments to their functioning continue to put patients and medical personnel at risk and undermine access to essential medical care. Against this backdrop, more than 100 states from all regions came together through the Global IHL Initiative to examine what meaningful protection for medical facilities requires in practice.

In this post, ICRC Legal Advisers Supriya Rao and Alexander Breitegger examine the recently released outcome document on Achieving Meaningful Protection for Medical Facilities in Conflict, resulting from several rounds of consultations with states led by Nigeria, Pakistan, Spain, Uruguay and the ICRC. This piece highlights key parts from the outcome document, including what the specific protection afforded to medical facilities entails, the strict conditions under which that protection may be lost, and the rules that continue to constrain attacks even when it is lost. Drawing on two years of state consultations and expert discussions, it also considers areas of disagreement among states and explains how the positions reflected in the outcome document can help states translate their existing legal obligations into meaningful protection on the ground.

Hospitals and other medical facilities enjoy one of the highest levels of protection under international humanitarian law (IHL), reflecting their life-saving function and going beyond the protection enjoyed by other civilian objects. Yet there is a widening gap between the protection the law provides and the grim reality on the ground, as attacks against health-care facilities, their misuse and impediments to their functioning continue to take a devastating toll. It was in response to this gap that the protection of medical facilities was chosen as one of the workstreams of the Global IHL Initiative.

Led by four co-chairing states – Nigeria, Pakistan, Spain and Uruguay – together with the ICRC, the workstream sought to reaffirm and deepen understanding of the existing IHL rules protecting medical facilities in contemporary armed conflict. It also aimed to identify practical measures, drawing on existing law and good practices from states, to strengthen implementation of those rules. The resulting outcome document, Achieving Meaningful Protection for Medical Facilities in Conflict, does not seek to create new law and is not open for endorsement. It reflects five consultations with more than 100 participating states from all regions of the world over 18 months, complemented by two expert workshops bringing together a wealth of experience and expertise.

At a time when hospitals are increasingly targeted or otherwise affected by hostilities, the outcome document provides an important reaffirmation of the specific protection IHL affords medical facilities. It examines what that protection requires in practice and offers states a concrete tool for translating their legal obligations into meaningful protection on the ground. In doing so, it demonstrates that respecting and protecting medical facilities during armed conflict is both possible and essential to fulfilling the fundamental obligation to care for the wounded and sick. It may also contribute to countering narratives and interpretations that portray the IHL rules protecting hospitals as significantly more flexible than they actually are.
articles.lede: When war reaches hospitals, protection becomes a matter of life and death. Discover what international humanitarian law demands.

articles.title: After the ICJ ruling, who pays? Vanuatu’s fight for climate justice premieres at COP31
6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Genocide in the Canvas? International Law and the Destruction of Lumière in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Genocide in the Canvas? International Law and the Destruction of Lumière in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
articles.description: [Dr Laurence Atkin-Teillet is a Lecturer in International Criminal and Humanitarian Law at Nottingham Law School, Nottingham Trent University.] What makes a world real? Is it the material from whic…
paragraphs: [ Dr Laurence Atkin-Teillet is a Lecturer in International Criminal and Humanitarian Law at Nottingham Law School, Nottingham Trent University.]

What makes a world real? Is it the material from which it is made, the person who created it, or the lives of those who inhabit it? And if a world contains beings who think, love, suffer, build communities and fear their own destruction, does it matter that they were painted into existence rather than born?

These questions are at the heart of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, the role-playing game developed by Sandfall Interactive. They also raise a very difficult question for international law: could the deliberate destruction of an entire population of human-like beings constitute genocide, even if those beings exist inside a painting?

The answer under existing international law is obviously not straightforward. Yet the question does show some important assumptions about the groups whom international law protects, the nature of personhood, and the boundaries between what we consider real and what we consider worthy of legal protection.

At first, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 appears to tell a story of a population living under the shadow of an existential threat. Its inhabitants live in Lumière, a city in a strange and beautiful world shaped by magic.

Each year, a figure known as the Paintress marks a new number on a distant Monolith. This number determines the age of those who will disappear in an event known as the Gommage. When the number changes to 33, everyone aged 33 vanishes, leaving families and friends to mourn those they have lost. Expedition 33 sets out to stop the Paintress and end the cycle. As the story continues, however, the distinction between reality and fiction begins to disappear.

The Canvas is not an imaginary world inhabited by characters who exist for the entertainment of an audience – it is a world created through the artistic powers of the Dessendre family. The real-world painter Verso created the Canvas; following his death, his mother, Aline, retreated into it and recreated aspects of the family she had lost. The world came to contain painted versions of people, alongside other beings with their own lives and identities.

Aline’s husband, Renoir, enters the Canvas in an attempt to bring her back to reality. Their conflict gradually threatens the survival of the world and its inhabitants. The struggle becomes even more complicated when we discover that Maelle is the real-world Alicia, who entered the Canvas and lost her former identity, while the painted Verso is a recreation of the real Verso.

The game’s ending presents a difficult choice. In Verso’s ending, often nicknamed the “ Genocide Ending ”, he defeats Maelle and destroys the Canvas. The painted world and the inhabitants whom the player has come to know disappear. In Maelle’s ending, she preserves the Canvas, but her decision also raises questions about autonomy and the right to determine one’s own existence.

The choice is between two understandings of what makes a life worth preserving. The painted inhabitants may have been created by another person, but they experience relationships, loss, fear and attachment – their lives have meaning to them. From their perspective, the destruction of the Canvas is the end of their world.
articles.lede: Is it the material from which it is made, the person who created it, or the lives of those who inhabit it?

articles.title: 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Who Can Speak for Earth? Representative Authority and First-Contact Governance in The Three-Body Problem
6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Who Can Speak for Earth? Representative Authority and First-Contact Governance in The Three-Body Problem
cats: Declaration of Principles Concerning the Conduct of the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence
articles.description: [Shaoxuan Xu is a PhD student in international law at Fudan University Law School and holds an LLM from New York University School of Law.] When Ye Wenjie receives an extraterrestrial warning, she …
paragraphs: [ Shaoxuan Xu is a PhD student in international law at Fudan University Law School and holds an LLM from New York University School of Law.]

When Ye Wenjie receives an extraterrestrial warning, she already has the means to answer. The warning tells her that replying will let the Trisolarans locate Earth and bring conquest, yet she responds. Later, Mike Evans finances a second communications base aboard Judgment Day. Control of the channel allows two people to make choices whose consequences extend far beyond themselves (chs. 24 and 29). Read alongside public governance documents, these episodes from the trilogy’s first volume raise a question that precedes the invasion: how does control over communication acquire the appearance of authority to represent everyone affected? I argue that first-contact governance must address both representative claims and the conditions for collective decision-making. Even a sender without authority can alter everyone else’s circumstances. Scrutiny of representative claims must therefore accompany procedures that preserve an opportunity for collective consideration before transmission changes the choices available.

Although Red Coast gives Ye the equipment to receive and answer signals, receiving a signal, authorizing transmission, choosing its content and claiming to speak for humanity remain distinct decisions. Scientific verification assesses a signal’s extraterrestrial origin, while an equipment license permits specified activities under the relevant rules. Neither determination alone establishes who may choose a reply or whose position the reply expresses. Even where one institution performs several functions, authority for one task does not automatically extend to the others. The distinction between privilege and legal power explains why. A privilege denotes the absence of a duty not to act in a particular legal relationship; a power is a legally recognized ability to alter legal relations. Equipment ownership, technical ability and permission to operate therefore cannot be treated as interchangeable with representative authority. A license concerned with technical compliance does not itself establish a mandate to make political commitments. Constitutional reasoning directs attention to the source, subject matter and limits of that authority: who conferred the power, what decision does it cover, and to whom must its exercise be explained?

Replacing an individual with a state does not settle the scope of representation. Under Principle 4 of the International Law Commission’s Guiding Principles Applicable to Unilateral Declarations of States Capable of Creating Legal Obligations (2006), a declaration binds a state only when a competent authority makes it. Principle 9 prevents one state’s declaration from imposing obligations on other states without their clear acceptance. These rules provide a structural comparison about authority among human actors; they do not determine the legal status of extraterrestrial communication. Authority to speak for one state cannot simply expand into authority to speak for humanity. The inquiry must identify who instructed the operator, what mandate the sending institution holds, and whom the final message represents. A signal’s physical reach answers none of those questions. Even a message addressed to the universe can express only a limited institutional position. Reaching a wider audience does not enlarge the constituency on whose behalf the sender is entitled to act.
articles.lede: When Ye Wenjie receives an extraterrestrial warning, she already has the means to answer. The warning tells her that replying will let the Trisolarans locate Earth and bring conquest, yet she responds.

articles.title: Fair Share Obligations in Climate Change Litigation: Towards a Global Carbon Approach?
Fair Share Obligations in Climate Change Litigation: Towards a Global Carbon Approach?
articles.description: In January of this year, the District Court of The Hague’s first-instance decision in Bonaire v The Netherlands found the Netherlands to be in violation of Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convent…
paragraphs: In January of this year, the District Court of The Hague’s first-instance decision in Bonaire v The Netherlands found the Netherlands to be in violation of Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention of Human Rights (“ECHR”) for failing to take sufficient climate mitigation and adaptation measures, resulting in discrimination towards the inhabitants of Bonaire.

Bonaire is among an increasing number of domestic court decisions that interpret human and constitutional rights in light of the international climate treaties to require each State to play their “part” or contribute their “fair share” in the mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions. Such language has its origins in the early Urgenda decision of 2019, which first put forward the concept of “partial responsibility” in the context of emission reductions: “each country is responsible for its part and can therefore be called to account in that respect” (para. 5.7.5). In adopting such logic, domestic courts globally reject the drop in the ocean argument in which individual responsibility for climate harm is diluted merely because emissions are cumulative in nature ( see decisions in Australia, Belgium, Germany, and Korea ).

While still under appeal, the District Court in Bonaire took this reasoning a step further. In its assessment of Article 8 of the ECHR, the District Court considered it a negative factor that the Netherlands had not quantified its emission allowance based on the remaining global carbon budget to limit global warming to 1.5°C (para. 11.15). In assessing whether the Netherlands had sufficiently played its part in emission reductions, it endorsed a global carbon budget approach.

This post draws attention to an increasing number of domestic courts that hold governments accountable for their failure to quantify their “fair share” of emissions in line with the global carbon budget. The first part defines the global carbon budget approach with reference to the reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (“IPCC”). The second unpacks the legal reasoning of recent domestic and regional court decisions that require States to determine their “fair share” on this basis. The third examines domestic courts’ engagement with the best available science to determine methodological considerations for calculating their “fair share” of emissions apportioned to the global carbon budget. It thereby points to an emerging practice of establishing responsibility for States’ due diligence obligations to reduce emissions commensurate with global mitigation efforts and fairness considerations, without necessarily evidencing a direct causal nexus with environmental harm.

The IPCC has estimated with a 50% probability that to keep greenhouse gas emission reductions in line with the 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, only 500 GtCO 2 remains available to be released into the atmosphere from 1 st January 2020 (p. 678). Under the global carbon budget approach, States collectively had a finite quantity of CO 2 in 2020 – exactly 500 GtCO 2 – that can be used in the transition to net-zero by 2050. Thus, for a State to contribute its “fair share”, it must carve out its share of remaining emissions from the global carbon budget consistently with its obligations under the international climate change regime, such as the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (“CBDR”) and set emission reduction targets accordingly.

articles.title: Mind the Gap: The Distance Between WHO Data and International Legal Standards
articles.description: Recent report concludes that WHO attack data cannot support the legal and comparative claims routinely built on top of it.
paragraphs: International lawyers, UN bodies, and human rights organizations increasingly cite one source when they discuss violence against health care in armed conflict: the World Health Organization’s Surveillance System on Attacks on Health Care (SSA). Since its launch in 2017, the SSA has become the default empirical basis for claims about the scale and pattern of harm caused to hospitals, clinics, medical transport, and health personnel in dozens of conflicts. The UN Office of the Special Representative for the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict draws on it. Special rapporteurs cite it. Advocacy organizations build their own datasets on top of it. It now shapes the narrative of accountability for alleged attacks on health care and forms the basis for misplaced arguments about culpability for them as breaches of international humanitarian standards.

We spent months reviewing the SSA’s methodology and publicly available data. Our conclusion—in a report recently published by The Hague Initiative for International Cooperation and the Henry Jackson Society—is that the system, as currently designed, cannot support the legal and comparative claims routinely built on top of it. This is not an argument against monitoring attacks on health care, which is an important and legitimate project. It is an argument that continuing to treat SSA figures as verified, comparable, or legally dispositive risks distorting the debate it’s meant to inform.

The SSA defines an “attack” as “any act of verbal or physical violence, threat of violence or other psychological violence, or obstruction that interferes with the availability, access and delivery of curative and/or preventive health services.” This is considerably broader than the operative legal definition of “attack” found in Additional Protocol I, Article 49, which requires an “act of violence against the adversary” connected to an armed conflict.

The over-extension matters. The SSA’s event taxonomy includes categories such as “psychological” violence (insults, intimidation, threats) and “obstruction,” which by the WHO’s own methodology can include a health worker being delayed at a security checkpoint, which is not an “act of violence.” It also includes arrests, detentions, and searches; categories of State and non-State conduct that international humanitarian law (IHL) does not automatically treat as unlawful, and that may in some circumstances be required by a party’s obligation to take precautions against the misuse of medical facilities. Some of this conduct is problematic, but labeling all of it “attack,” without further qualification, imports a legal conclusion the underlying facts don’t establish.

We also found, using conflict-onset data from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, that 39% of logged SSA events in the occupied Palestinian territory occurred during periods that would not meet standard thresholds for active armed conflict, a precondition for the legal category of “attack” to apply at all. This suggests the SSA is, at least in part, capturing lower-level friction and violence. Such conduct is distinct from attacks governed by IHL.
articles.lede: Recent report concludes that WHO attack data cannot support the legal and comparative claims routinely built on top of it.

articles.title: 25ème session de l’Assemblée des États Parties au Statut de Rome de la Cour pénale internationale, du 30 novembre au 7 décembre 2026 (AEP25)
25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma de la Corte Penal Internacional
25th session of the ICC Assembly of States Parties, 30 November
25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma de la Corte Penal Internacional, del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026 (AEP25)
articles.description: Share this page Twitter Twitter Twitter Mail EN
paragraphs: Del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026, los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma se reunirán en La Haya con motivo de la 25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes de la Corte Penal Internacional (AEP25).

La Asamblea es el órgano de supervisión y legislativo de la Corte. Reunidos en sesión plenaria una vez al año, los Estados Partes adoptan decisiones fundamentales para el funcionamiento eficaz de la Corte y del sistema del Estatuto de Roma en su conjunto.

La AEP25 se celebra en un momento crítico para la justicia internacional. Ante la intensificación de los ataques contra la CPI, sus funcionarios, las organizaciones de la sociedad civil y otras personas y entidades que apoyan su mandato, la Asamblea brinda a los Estados Partes una oportunidad esencial para demostrar, mediante medidas concretas, su compromiso con una Corte independiente y eficaz y para proteger la integridad del sistema del Estatuto de Roma.

La sociedad civil estará presente durante toda la sesión para seguir los debates, dialogar con los Estados Partes y los funcionarios de la Corte y abogar por una CPI justa, eficaz e independiente, procurando al mismo tiempo que las perspectivas de las víctimas, las personas supervivientes y quienes defienden los derechos humanos sigan ocupando un lugar central en las deliberaciones sobre justicia y rendición de cuentas.

En su vigésima quinta sesión, la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma (AEP) elegirá a seis jueces/juezas para cubrir un tercio de los 18 puestos de magistrado de la Corte Penal Internacional, conforme al ciclo electoral trienal ordinario. Cada uno/a de los/as seis jueces/juezaselegidos ejercerá un mandato de nueve años, de 2027 a 2036.

Las elecciones judiciales figuran entre las funciones de gobernanza más importantes de la Asamblea. La calidad, independencia y diversidad de los magistrados de la Corte inciden directamente en la credibilidad de la CPI, el desarrollo de su jurisprudencia y su desempeño operativo. El Estatuto de Roma establece un marco jurídico detallado destinado a garantizar que los magistrados sean seleccionados en función de sus méritos, integridad y representatividad, mientras que las resoluciones posteriores de la Asamblea han reforzado progresivamente las salvaguardias de transparencia y diligencia debida.

En vísperas de la AEP25, organizaciones de la sociedad civil y personas defensoras de los derechos humanos de todas las regiones comparten sus prioridades y recomendaciones para fortalecer la justicia a través de la CPI y del sistema del Estatuto de Roma.

Estas contribuciones son mucho más que declaraciones: reflejan las realidades vividas por quienes se encuentran en primera línea de los esfuerzos de rendición de cuentas. A lo largo de la AEP25, #NGOVoices seguirá dando visibilidad a estas perspectivas, para que las decisiones adoptadas en La Haya reflejen las necesidades y los conocimientos de quienes trabajan por la justicia en todo el mundo.
En los márgenes de la AEP25, la sociedad civil, los Estados, la Corte y otros actores organizan numerosos eventos paralelos.
articles.lede: Del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026, los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma se reunirán en La Haya con motivo de la 25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes de la Corte Penal Internacional (AEP25).

Egypt: Fact-checking site’s entire newsroom jailed as assault on press freedom widens
articles.description: Six journalists who make up the entire newsroom of the Egyptian fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention, the UN human rights office (OHCHR) said on Tuesday, warning of proliferating assaults on press freedom by the Government.
paragraphs: “ We are witnessing widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists ,” the human rights chief’s spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan told journalists in Geneva.
“ These alarming developments must end immediately, and journalists must be able to carry out their essential work free from intimidation and reprisals.”

The detained reporters are Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Abdallah Qadry, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohamed Mahmoud and Mohamed Adel. According to their lawyers, they were tortured and otherwise ill-treated and forced to record fabricated confessions.
Lina Attalah, chief editor of the independent online news outlet Mada Masr, also faces continuing judicial harassment linked to her journalistic work, the OHCHR spokesperson said.
Last month, an Egyptian court convicted her of operating an unlicensed website. She was detained, then released after paying a fine, and the court ordered the website closed.
This week, she faces another hearing in a separate case dating back to 2024 – raising fresh concerns over legal due process and the right to a fair trial, including obstacles to appeal.
OHCHR called on Egypt to end all forms of harassment of journalists and media outlets, and to respect and fulfil the right to freedom of expression, including the right to information.

The authorities must release all the Matsadash reporters and drop charges arising from their legitimate journalistic work, the UN rights office said. Until then, they must have confidential access to lawyers, contact with their families, necessary healthcare and medication, and humane conditions of detention.
“ All allegations of torture, ill-treatment or forced confessions must be promptly investigated, and those responsible held to account ,” Mr. Al-Kheetan said.
articles.lede: Six journalists who make up the entire newsroom of the Egyptian fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention, the UN human rights office (OHCHR) said on Tuesday, warning of proliferating assaults on press freedom…

articles.title: Sudan war: First ‘suicide’ drone attacks, now long-range strikes are the norm
articles.description: Drones and drought are “closing in” on Sudan, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), said on Tuesday, describing unprecedented attacks on the country’s infrastructure including by drones travelling up to 1,500 kilometres before hitting their target.
paragraphs: “It is an assault unlike anything Sudan has seen before. In the last week of October, not a single day passed without a drone strike on a power station in Sudan. Up to 15 were hit in the month of October,” said agency spokesperson James Elder.

“This year in Sudan, two in three child casualties were killed by armed drones. They are bringing war to places that were once safe. People in Sudan talk about three things: they talk about safety, education and water. Drones are taking all three .”
The UNICEF alert comes amid ongoing fighting between former allies turned military rivals the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

Well over 15 million people urgently require shelter across the country but drone strikes on civilians, markets and key public infrastructure continue to hinder aid efforts and increase the suffering of non-combatants.
“Several years ago, there was a use of suicide drones, which was terrifying to see that in Sudan,” Mr. Elder explained.

Highlighting the use of increasingly accurate long-range drones in the last 12 months, including some travelling 1,500 kilometres, he explained that it was impossible for humanitarian agencies like UNICEF to ascertain who was behind “at least 15 strikes” on Sudanese power stations in October. “One would struggle to think if it was in the interest of the SAF, of Government, to do that,” he added.

Straight off the plane from Sudan, Mr. Elder told journalists in Geneva about one of the many young war victims he had met from El Obeid, where UN Human Rights Council investigators say that civilians live in constant fear of drone attack.

“Buri is a teenager. An explosive took both his hands. He lives in a tent. He told me, ‘I must accept this,’” Mr. Elder explained. “ He spends the mornings learning online and the afternoons picking grass for animals with stumps for hands. His friends help him, that’s Sudan. It’s relentless. It’s crushing .”

Like Ukraine, Sudan’s energy sector is being struck repeatedly, but unlike in Ukraine, Sudanese targets are not repaired, the UNICEF spokesperson stressed: “When a power station is struck, water pumps stop, water treatment stops. Families are forced into expensive and unsafe alternatives.”
articles.lede: Drones and drought are “closing in” on Sudan, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), said on Tuesday, describing unprecedented attacks on the country’s infrastructure including by drones travelling up to 1,500 kilometres…

articles.title: The legal battle over a torture centre in Kupiansk
articles.description: In northern Ukraine, a trial concerning the Russian “torture centre” in Kupiansk is unprecedented, involving dozens of victims and 18 defendants, according to the regional prosecutor’s office. But the case is struggling to make headway.
paragraphs: “I lost 18 kilos in there, and came out with grey hair,” says Larisa Fesenko, 63-year-old head and English teacher at Lisnistenkiv Secondary School in Lista Stinka, which is in the Kupiansk region of north-east Ukraine. During the Russian occupation of 2022, she spent nearly 45 days in the cells of the Kupiansk police station. According to the Ukrainian police and public prosecutor’s office, this was where one of the largest Russian torture centres in the Kharkiv region was located.

Fesenko is one of 87 victims in the Koupiansk torture centre case. Arrested on July 26, 2022, she was put in a cramped cell, where 10 to 20 other detainees were crammed onto a concrete floor covered with linoleum. “In July, the Russians abducted me straight from my home. They put a bag over my head, handcuffed me, and then took me to the torture centre,” she recounts. “I remember that day, July 26, and I will never forget it.”

The reason for her arrest? During a search of her home, the Russians found Ukrainian symbols, including a national flag that this head teacher had brought back from her school. Whilst she was striving to preserve the school’s heritage and maintain team cohesion, some of her colleagues chose to collaborate with the aggressor, according to her own account. “I was told that I would not be released under any circumstances, because I had arrived there with symbols. I was one of the political prisoners,” Fesenko continues.

The teacher says she did not betray her convictions, maintaining a pro-Ukrainian stance both at the time of her arrest and during interrogations. And she considers herself lucky: unlike others, she was subjected to neither physical violence nor electric shocks during her two interrogations, only sometimes threatened with sending her “to Belgorod” (a Russian city across the border to the north of Kharkiv), or putting her “among the deserters”. “The air in the cell was stifling. No light filtered through the windows, and we weren’t taken out into the open air,” she recalls. “We were barely fed – just noodles twice a day.”

“My place was on the floor, between two bunk beds. The toilet was in the same room,” says Fesenko. “Two people were on the bunk beds, but everyone else was on the floor – some under the beds, others near the toilet. Industrial water ran from the tap. We used it to wash and to drink.”

According to the prosecutor’s office, the arrests were unfounded and the guards forced prisoners to sing the Russian national anthem, punched and kicked them, and subjected them to electric shocks. “After the electric shocks, I had an operation on my hands. But I still haven’t regained full sensation. My hands haven’t fully regained their function,” says one of the victims quoted by the Kharkiv regional prosecutor’s office.

“At night, we could constantly hear footsteps in the corridor. They were taking people away. We sat there and could hear someone being tortured,” recalls the teacher. “The cells were open, and we could hear everything. A young man was beaten until he lost his voice, until he fell completely silent. Can you imagine? And it was like that every night.”
articles.lede: In northern Ukraine, a trial concerning the Russian “torture centre” in Kupiansk is unprecedented, involving dozens of victims and 18 defendants, according to the regional prosecutor’s office. But the case is struggling to make headway.

articles.title: Eyes in the sky, weapons in hand: FPV drones and the challenges for IHL and the protection of civilians
articles.description: FPV drones, IHL compliance and the growing challenges of protecting civilians in armed conflict.
paragraphs: Drones have become a defining feature of contemporary armed conflicts. Their use has surged dramatically in recent years, originally with the proliferation of inexpensive, commercially available systems, and increasingly with militaries also manufacturing drones at scale. Among these, first-person view (FPV) drones – small, agile aircraft controlled by an operator with a live video stream directly from the drone’s camera – have emerged as a particularly versatile tool. Small, cheap, and easy to assemble and operate, FPV drones have reportedly been used by both state and non-state armed actors in conflicts across all regions of the world, including in Latin America, Gaza, Syria, Iran and elsewhere in West Asia, the Sahel (e.g. Mali ), Sudan, Ukraine, Thailand and Cambodia, and Myanmar.

In this post, ICRC Advisers Georgia Hinds, Mauro Vignati and Eirini Giorgou examine how FPV drones are reshaping the conduct of hostilities, with implications for civilians in armed conflict and for compliance with international humanitarian law (IHL). They go on to suggest practical measures that parties to armed conflict should take to address these risks and ensure respect for IHL.

The term “first-person view” has its roots in video games of the 1970s, in which the player could experience the game through the eyes of a character. Originally developed for civilian use, particularly hobby flying and drone racing, FPV drones are characterized by a front-facing camera transmitting live footage to the operator, enabling immersive control beyond line of sight. This relatively simple innovation has made FPV drones highly adaptable for military use. Technological improvements – enhanced maneuverability, increased payload capacity, extended range or flight time, and the integration of thermal cameras – have further expanded their operational utility.

Recent developments also point toward increasing autonomy. Some FPV drones can continue flying toward a pre-designated target even when communication with the operator is disrupted. While autonomy in navigation on its own does not make an FPV drone an autonomous weapon system, it illustrates a broader trend toward reduced human involvement in certain functions.
These drones are now used for both surveillance and attack, often in combination with other systems, in addition to less traditional tasks such as the acceptance of surrender by adversaries. [1]

FPV drones are increasingly used to carry out attacks in armed conflict. They are typically armed with explosive payloads which are then dropped onto targets or detonate when the drone crashes into a target. They can be used individually or in coordinated swarms to target personnel or equipment. Whilst FPV drones are still predominantly “multirotor” configurations, fixed-wing models are increasingly being used to extend range, speed and payload capacity, with reported examples of operational range now reaching 30 kilometers.

Some FPV drones may “loiter” for periods of time. They can be used in ambush-style operations, kept concealed until a target appears and the operator detonates the munition. Others are reported to be configured to detonate upon movement or tampering. It is extremely difficult to verify these claims and technical capabilities. But such “victim-activated” systems may qualify as mines or booby-traps, governed by the relevant treaty and customary IHL rules, or as autonomous weapon systems if they can select and engage a target based on its movement without further human intervention, in which case the ICRC’s recommendations on autonomous weapons are especially relevant.
articles.lede: FPV drones, IHL compliance and the growing challenges of protecting civilians in armed conflict.

articles.title: Generating the New World: A Critical Perspective on EJIL’s Policy on Gen AI Use
articles.description: Introduction EJIL’s first Policy on Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) was introduced in July 2026, with an editorial comment by Sarah Nouwen and Michael Waibel. Such Gen AI policie…
paragraphs: EJIL’s first Policy on Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) was introduced in July 2026, with an editorial comment by Sarah Nouwen and Michael Waibel. Such Gen AI policies have been adopted by major international law journals, such as AJIL, ICLQ, and LJIL under CUP’s policy, and JICJ, JCSL, and JIDS under OUP’s policy. The general trend is the obligation to disclose Gen AI use beyond minimal uses such as language checking, authors’ responsibility for manuscripts involving AI, and the denial of authorship to AI. The EJIL policy is apparently restrictive in its prohibition of certain ways of Gen AI use by introducing its human-AI outweighing approach (para. 3). One might question whether the policy really fits the reality of widespread Gen AI use, as already acknowledged by the policy’s statement that Gen AI ‘is increasingly being used in academic research and writing’ (para. 1).

Throughout human history, revolutionary technological developments have redefined what counts as necessary competencies for life and work, including scholarly work. Overly rigid policies on Gen AI use that pose a high or unclear hurdle for such use, in combination with the disclosure obligation and the possibility of severe sanctions, could have significant repercussions for other academic societies and journals, especially when adopted by prominent journals such as EJIL. This would risk hampering the necessary transformation of scholarly work.

Against this background, I venture to submit a fundamental critique of EJIL’s Gen AI policy. While Niccolò Ridi has already posted an excellent argument primarily about the enforcement aspect of the policy on this blog, my argument questions the underlying logic and premises of the policy, drawing on such concepts as dynamic interplay, absolute authorial accountability, and the transparency dilemma.

Let me clarify the structure of the policy. Paragraph 1 provides the statement of the principle that ‘while Gen AI may complement, it should not replace, human intelligence in scholarly production’, and paragraph 3(a) sets out two requirements: ‘the submission contains a significant intellectual contribution’ and ‘the intellectual contribution of the named author(s) clearly outweighs the contribution of Gen AI’. When Gen AI’s contribution, ‘if made by a human’, would warrant the status of a co-author, the outweighing test is not met (para. 3(a)(ii)). Those formulations are to be interpreted ‘by reference to legal-academic best practice on authorship and responsibility’ (para. 3(b)), based on an ‘analogy’, as explained by the editorial comment. There are two points to be made about this structure. First, it is doubtful that existing practice is clear enough to allow an objective assessment of whether a research assistant’s contribution deserves co-authorship or only acknowledgement, even in traditional settings involving only humans. The mere collection of relevant literature requires substantive, in some cases, normative judgements on what constitutes relevance in particular contexts. For me, Joseph Weiler’s emphasis on ab initio discussion with research assistants about co-authorship suggests the inherent difficulties, at least in legal scholarship, of leaving this to the determination of a third party, who was not involved in that research process.
articles.lede: EJIL’s first Policy on Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) was introduced in July 2026, with an editorial comment by Sarah Nouwen and Michael Waibel.

articles.title: Generating the New World: A Critical Perspective on EJIL’s Policy on Gen AI Use
How the UN Bought Time for the World to Understand Autonomous Weapons
articles.description: UN bought essential time for States and armed forces to reveal the principles and practices of AI-enabled LAWS.
paragraphs: As the UN Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) concludes its decade-long mandate on lethal autonomous weapon systems (LAWS), its final report does little more than reiterate existing International Humanitarian Law (IHL). However, its value should not be judged as a failed legal endeavour, but as a protracted holding pattern that absorbed public moral panic and protected against premature vetoes or restrictions. In delaying top-down regulation, it bought essential time for States and armed forces to reveal the principles and practices of AI-enabled LAWS. This process provided opponents and proponents with technical ground truth rather than sci-fi hype.

The humanitarian risks from “Killer Robots” digitally dehumanising combatants and killing civilians dominated the public conscience in the early 2010s. The combination of uncrewed aircraft and emerging AI presented a fantastical science fiction threat that urgently needed to be controlled or banned. The GGE was established in 2017 to respond to concerns that existing controls were insufficient for novel LAWS.

As a mechanism to inform global regulation, the GGE’s initial progress appeared painfully slow, with huge effort expended just trying to define the problems it was meant to solve. In 2019, it agreed on eleven “ guiding principles” to shape the group’s work. In 2023 the UN Secretary General called on world leaders to launch negotiations of a new legally binding instrument, with the GGE mandated to formulate the “set of elements” to guide this future work. As the 2026 Report concludes this task of international consensus-building and prepares the ground for even more negotiations, we must ask whether the GGE’s involvement was necessary or desirable?

The panic surrounding LAWS made political outsourcing inevitable. Orben’s The Sisyphean Cycle of Technology Panics highlights political distancing as an established and typical response to threats from new technology. The cycle’s first stage, “panic creation,” is characterised by actors highlighting the risks of new technology in broad, and often misleading, terms. For LAWS, this included the Stop Killer Robots Campaigners’ Kit, which helped create widespread fear of autonomous killing.

This moral panic then feeds the second stage, “political outsourcing,” whereby politicians push the debate to external contestation. LAWS contestation was outsourced to the GGE and its multinational, NGO and scientific membership.

Despite the GGE’s protracted contestation, its eventual consensus has produced very little that is different from the prohibitions and restrictions already in place for other weapons. The overwhelming majority of the report can therefore be seen as standard weapons controls.

In the report, IHL remains the central principle for LAWS use, and there are a few LAWS-specific elements to guide their design. For example, software must be locked down and understood, operational effects must be limitable, and a human must be responsible and accountable for each use. The requirement that “those responsible for the use of LAWS can limit their effects” is already a fundamental requirement of command and control.
articles.lede: UN bought essential time for States and armed forces to reveal the principles and practices of AI-enabled LAWS.

articles.description: On 3 November 2026, the UN Security Council and General Assembly met concurrently to fill five vacancies on the International Court of Justice (ICJ). This was the first election since 2017 in which…
paragraphs: On 3 November 2026, the UN Security Council and General Assembly met concurrently to fill five vacancies on the International Court of Justice (ICJ). This was the first election since 2017 in which no seat held by a non-P5 member of WEOG (Western European and Others Group) fell vacant. In 2020, the term of Giorgio Gaja (Italy) was ending, and in 2023, so were those of Hilary Charlesworth (Australia) and Joan Donoghue (United States). In this election, for the nine-year term beginning 2027, the only WEOG vacancy was the seat held by Ronny Abraham (France), while the other four fell to the Asia-Pacific group (Dalveer Bhandari from India, leaving; Mahmoud Daifallah Hmoud from Jordan, seeking re-election), Africa (Phoebe Okowa from Kenya, seeking re-election), and Latin America (Leonardo Nemer Caldeira Brant from Brazil, leaving). Assuming that France would retain the seat vacated by Abraham, in keeping with the conventional distribution of seats among regional groups and the P5, the UK’s nomination of Dapo Akande, the Nigerian-British professor, therefore raised the possibility of displacing a candidate from another regional group.

Akande and Ambassador François Alabrune (both from P5 countries and WEOG) had the most nominations, with 43 and 40 respectively, followed by Singaporean Ambassador Rena Lee, who received nominations from 33 states across regional groups. Seeking re-election, Okowa (Kenya) and Hmoud had 26 and 15 nominations respectively. The number of nominations was partly reflected in the first-round voting of both organs, in which Lee (151 in the Assembly and 13 in the Council), Alabrune (146 in the Assembly and 13 in the Council), and Akande (129 in the Assembly and 11 in the Council) were the top three picks. Hmoud secured majorities (106 in the Assembly and 10 in the Council), but Okowa, despite securing a majority in the Assembly (117 votes), fell 2 votes short in the Council (6 votes). Meanwhile, Marcelo Vázquez-Bermúdez, the Ecuadorian Ambassador who is also a member of the International Law Commission and Special Rapporteur for General Principles of Law, secured the required majority in the Council (9 votes) but not in the Assembly (73 votes). As Article 10 of the ICJ Statute requires candidates to obtain an absolute majority in both organs to be elected, neither Okowa nor Vázquez-Bermúdez could therefore secure the fifth seat.

Lee and Hmoud both secured the required majorities in the two organs, meaning that the Asia-Pacific group would retain four seats on the Court, alongside the two incumbents, Iwasawa Yuji and Xue Hanqin. The extent of overlapping support for the region’s candidates is also noteworthy. In the Security Council, each member had five votes, and Lee and Hmoud received 13 and 10 votes respectively. Since there were only 15 members, at least 8 (13+10-15) must have voted for both. In the General Assembly, the combined votes for Lee, Hmoud and Paik amounted to 349. Of the 191 states that cast valid ballots, at least 79 ([349-191]/2) must therefore have voted for two or more of the three Asian candidates. These are minimum figures, since the ballots were secret and the actual overlap may have been higher. Although states may have supported these candidates on the basis of their individual qualifications rather than regional considerations, the figures suggest that there was no widespread reluctance to see the Asia-Pacific group retain its existing representation, even with two additional seats at stake in this election. While the British and French candidates also commanded considerable support, the remaining question was who would be left out.
articles.lede: On 3 November 2026, the UN Security Council and General Assembly met concurrently to fill five vacancies on the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

articles.title: Beyond the broken glass: The human cost of the 1938 November Pogrom
articles.description: On his way to school in Vienna on the morning of 10 November 1938, eight-year-old Arthur Schneier watched his synagogue burn while firefighters and police officers stood by “rejoicing”.
paragraphs: More than 87 years later, Rabbi Schneier told a UN panel in New York that the memory has never left him.

It shaped a lifelong conviction, he said in a video recording: an attack on a community’s house of worship strikes at the very heart of its faith. His message was one of mutual respect and acceptance, and a call for everyone to learn from the past.

The panel was held this week ahead of the 88th anniversary of the Kristallnacht pogrom, when years of State-sponsored antisemitism erupted into orchestrated violence against Jewish communities across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland.
Speakers set out to look past the familiar images of shattered shop windows to the fear, grief and loss lived by Jewish children, parents and neighbours.
On the night of 9–10 November 1938, synagogues were set alight, Jewish homes and businesses were ransacked and some 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps.

It marked a turning point: Nazi persecution of Jews moved from discrimination and exclusion to open violence on the streets. Many tried to flee, only to find that other countries would not take them in.

The Nazis called it Kristallnacht – “crystal night”, or the night of broken glass. The name came from the shards that littered the streets, but it was a euphemism that played down the violence done to people.
The photographs remain: Jewish men forced to march through their towns with their heads uncovered; neighbours looking on; synagogues desecrated; homes and businesses ransacked.
But what do these images really tell us about the people who lived through the pogrom? And what do they leave out?
articles.lede: On his way to school in Vienna on the morning of 10 November 1938, eight-year-old Arthur Schneier watched his synagogue burn while firefighters and police officers stood by “rejoicing”.

articles.description: 1. Call for Submissions: The Board of Peace and its Role in International Law – Challenge, Continuity or a New Global Legal Order? The Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and Inte…
paragraphs: 1. Call for Submissions: The Board of Peace and its Role in International Law – Challenge, Continuity or a New Global Legal Order? The Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law is inviting submissions for a workshop to be held on 5 February 2027 on The Board of Peace and its role in international law: Challenge, continuity or a new global legal order? Looking back at the first year of the Board of Peace’s existence, this workshop intends to explore whether the Board challenges or even violates international law, how far it is genuinely new in the governance of peace, security and peacebuilding, and what to expect from it in the coming years, given its limited activity so far. They welcome papers from a variety of legal and interdisciplinary perspectives, particularly from Early Career Researchers. Abstracts should be submitted by 30 November 2026. The full CfP can be found here.

2. Caititu: A Free Research Tool for Inter-American Human Rights Case Law. Caititu connects AI chats, such as Claude and ChatGPT, to a structured database of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights: about 630 judgments and advisory opinions, with footnotes, separate opinions, summaries and the Cuadernillos de Jurisprudencia. Its aim is to make AI research less opaque and more reliable: instead of relying on training data or random web searches, the chat consults the official texts and receives each passage with its case and paragraph number, so that it can be checked. You can ask in any language. Caititu offers lexical and semantic search, traces the genealogy of a standard, and shows who cited a paragraph and what the Court drew from the European Court, UN treaty bodies and other sources. Built from public, official sources, it is meant for research, not drafting. It is currently in beta. Details here.

3. Call for Papers: Reparations for Harm – Intersections of Human Rights, Humanitarian and International Criminal Law: The Workshop ‘Reparations for Harm: Intersections of Human Rights, Humanitarian and International Criminal Law’ will be held in Utrecht on 22 – 23 April 2027. The rapidly changing geopolitical landscape and large-scale armed conflicts underscore the need for victim reparation for serious human rights violations and other violations of international humanitarian or criminal law. The workshop will host several panels on all aspects of reparations. The convenors encourage submissions on (but not limited to): reparations by human rights courts and quasi-judicial mechanisms, reparations in international criminal justice, reparations for harm in inter-state and mass claims mechanisms, reparations for harm before domestic courts, and universal jurisdiction and reparations. For more information and submission guidelines, see the CfP here.

4. Digital Dual Use Conference. The ZEVEDI project group ‘Digital Dual Use’ will host an interdisciplinary conference in Frankfurt am Main on 3 – 4 December 2026. ‘Dual use’ refers to the possibility that civilian technologies could be used for hostile military purposes. When applied to digital solutions and goods, this concept reaches its limits, raising the question of whether the existing dual-use framework needs to be reconsidered. At the conference, both the existing legal framework and the specific characteristics of digital technologies will be discussed, and an analysis will be carried out to explain why digital issues can present challenges for dual-use assessments. The conference will be held in German. You can find the conference programme and registration details here.
articles.lede: Call for Submissions: The Board of Peace and its Role in International Law – Challenge, Continuity or a New Global Legal Order?

GC IV Commentary Series – Article 47 of the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949: A Possible Blind Spot
articles.description: The interpretation of Article 47 of GC IV raises a general legal issue: the proper balance between rigidity and flexibility.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

Although the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) updated Commentary offers thorough treatment, the aim of this post is to cast additional light on two sides of the coin that is Article 47 of the 1949 Fourth Geneva Convention (GC IV). First, we will explore the true scope and content of the provision to give it proper interpretation.

Second, we will consider whether there are some situations for which the regulation of Article 47 is not fully adapted, namely, situations which lead to a normative blind spot. This may be the case especially in prolonged occupations, where agreements must to some extent adapt the situation to new realities. The aim of these agreements must not be to deprive civilians of their rights, although exactly that may incidentally occur to some extent. Would then Article 47 entail a responsibility of the parties to the agreement, or even cause it to become void? This question is explored here to supplement the coverage offered by the updated Commentary.

Protected persons who are in occupied territory shall not be deprived, in any case or in any manner whatsoever, of the benefits of the present Convention by any change introduced, as the result of the occupation of a territory, into the institutions or government of the said territory, nor by any agreement concluded between the authorities of the occupied territories and the Occupying Power, nor by any annexation by the latter of the whole or part of the occupied territory.

The article aims to maintain the legal effectiveness of the rights and especially the obligations incumbent upon an occupying power (i.e. the rights of the civilians in occupied territory). An occupant may well be tempted by an all-too-easy pretext to evade its duties as occupier if it could, for example, annex the territory and pretend that, being now on its own national territory, it would not owe obligations under the law of occupation. The aim of Article 47 is thus to close the way to such circumventing action and to forestall a glaring and threatening gap in the law of occupation.
In this regard, Article 47 is fundamental. In the words of the recent updated ICRC GC IV Commentary,

Its placement underscores the importance of this rule, establishing as it does the inviolability of the benefits guaranteed by the Convention to protected persons in occupied territory and ensuring that they are not deprived of those benefits in any way. It is a key safeguard in relation to all the other provisions in the Convention that are applicable during occupation (para. 3097).

Despite its fundamental character, it must be recalled that Article 47 is a mere jus in bello provision without any jus ad bellum component. In this sense, Article 47 does not prohibit annexation of territory. The prohibition of annexation is contained in the jus ad bellum and is attached to Article 2(4) of the UN Charter. Instead, the point of Article 47 is merely to state that even if the described action takes place (e.g. an annexation occurs) protected persons cannot be stripped of their rights and the occupying power concomitantly does not free itself of its corresponding obligations.
articles.lede: The interpretation of Article 47 of GC IV raises a general legal issue: the proper balance between rigidity and flexibility.

articles.title: Afghanistan faces deepening humanitarian crisis amid sweeping rights restrictions
articles.description: Afghanistan stands at a “difficult crossroad” more than five years after the Taliban returned to power, a senior UN official said on Friday. Relative stability and security are being undercut by a fragile economy, sweeping curbs on rights and acute humanitarian need.
paragraphs: Bruno Lemarquis is the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Afghanistan. He is also the UN’s Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in the country.
Women and girls continue to suffer from “severe and sweeping” restrictions on their freedoms, being deprived of many spaces to learn, work and participate in public life, Mr. Lemarquis stressed.
In particular, the restriction of girls’ access to education represents “one of the world’s most sensitive…education challenges,” he said.
Since 2021, over 2.6 million girls have been denied secondary education, and female university enrollment currently stands at zero.
But higher education overall is in crisis: due to the country’s economic frailty, some families are also holding back from sending their boys to school.

When asked by a journalist how the Taliban justify their restrictions on women and girls, Mr. Lemarquis said their explanations are a mix of religious extremism and deep historical practices of control and discrimination.
Since September 2025, Afghan women staffers have also been banned from entering United Nations premises across the country, and the ban has not been lifted.
The “massive” return of 6.7 million nationals to Afghanistan since 2020 is also placing additional strain on its already stretched services.
Many were forcibly expelled from the neighbouring countries that were hosting them, with a large portion coming from Pakistan and Iran.
articles.lede: Afghanistan stands at a “difficult crossroad” more than five years after the Taliban returned to power, a senior UN official said on Friday.

articles.title: Syria: a map of trials since the fall of Assad
articles.description: Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime on December 8, 2024, the Syrian judiciary has brought charges against several dozen people accused of serious crimes committed under the former regime and since the start of the transition.
paragraphs: These promises of justice come as a response to strong demands from the Syrian people and the international community. Hearings have been held in Damascus and Aleppo, some of which have received extensive media coverage. Public prosecutors’ offices dedicated to transitional justice cases are being established in Homs and Latakia. Proceedings are not all held in the same way: some are public, others take place behind closed doors, and several defendants are being tried in absentia. Here we list the criminal proceedings that are currently known, almost two years after Assad’s fall.

Below, Justice Info presents a map accompanied by a summary of the figures and visual data. All of this data (finalised in early November 2026) is set out in more detail in an article further down the page.

On November 18, 2025, the trial began concerning violence that struck the Syrian coast in March 2025, resulting in more than 1,400 deaths among Alawite civilians. This trial in Aleppo (north-west Syria) represents a response by the current government to the massacres. Seven militiamen loyal to the former regime and seven members of the new security forces were tried over the course of 16 hearings, held both in public and in camera. On September 17 and October 15, 2026, the military court handed down 11 convictions and 2 acquittals.

In 2026, the Syrian capital has seen several trials organised on crimes attributed to former officials and leading figures of the Assad regime, including Bashar al-Assad himself. The majority are being heard by the Fourth Criminal Chamber of the Damascus Courthouse.

• On April 26, 2026, the Fourth Criminal Chamber in Damascus opened its first major trial, with Atef Najib, former head of political security in Deraa (southern Syria), Bashar al-Assad and seven other officials being tried in absentia. They include the former president’s brother Maher Hafez al-Assad and former defence minister Fahd Jassem al-Freij. Najib, who was arrested on April 7, 2026, appeared at nine hearings. The court heard dozens of witnesses with regard to the arrest and alleged torture of children, shooting of demonstrators, and events that took place at the al-Omari Mosque. On August 11, 2026, the court delivered its 396-page judgement. “The document will be published at a later date on the Ministry of Justice’s official website, once the names of protected witnesses have been redacted,” the official Syrian news agency Sana stated in a press release. The court found Najib guilty of murder and ordering the shooting of demonstrators. It described the acts as crimes against humanity and sentenced him to death. On the same day, the court handed down death sentences in absentia against Bashar al-Assad and seven other senior officials.
In a statement to Sana, Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan, president of the Fourth Criminal Chamber, announced that the judgments handed down in absentia would be forwarded to Interpol.

• On June 14, 2026, the trial of Abdel Nasser al-Burraqi began before the Fourth Criminal Chamber at the Damascus Courthouse. Described as an informant for the former regime, he was charged with enforced disappearance, arbitrary detention, complicity in premeditated murder, torture resulting in death, robbery with violence and false accusation. On August 27, 2026, he was found guilty of all these crimes. In classifying them as war crimes and crimes against humanity, the court drew on international law. It applied Syrian law in determining the sentence. Al-Burraqi was sentenced to death, with seizure of all his assets.

Liechtenstein Renews its Support to the Trust Fund for Victims through a Voluntary Contribution
articles.description: The Principality of Liechtenstein, a State Party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC) since 2001, has made voluntary contributions of EUR 52,470 to the Trust Fund for Victims (TFV) in 2026, reaffirming its commitment to international justice and the rights of victims of crimes under the Rome Statute. Liechtenstein's voluntary contribution is of an unrestricted nature and will be used to redress the harm suffered by victims, through reparation awards ordered by the ICC and other programmes for their benefit. H.E. Kevin Kelly, Member of the Board of Directors of the TFV stated, “I express my sincere gratitude to Liechtenstein for its voluntary contribution. This contribution reflects a shared conviction that justice must extend beyond accountability and include concrete measures to address the harm suffered by victims. Particularly in these turbulent times for the Court, Liechtenstein's longstanding commitment helps deliver meaningful reparations and assistance, while ensuring that victims remain at the heart of the Rome Statute system."H.E. Christian Wenaweser, Permanent Representative of the Principality of Liechtenstein to the United Nations stated, “Liechtenstein remains firmly committed to the Trust Fund for Victims and its unique mission of supporting those who have become victims of the most serious crimes covered by the Rome Statute. At a time when the delivery of assistance, rehabilitation and reparations to victims faces growing challenges, it is more important than ever that the international community stands united behind the TFV. Through our continued contribution in 2026, we reaffirm our conviction that justice and accountability must include addressing the rights, needs and dignity of victims.”Liechtenstein has provided regular support to the TFV through voluntary contributions since 2005, demonstrating its long-standing commitment to supporting victims of the most serious crimes of international concern. Background information about the Trust Fund for VictimsVoluntary contributions to the TFV enable the delivery of the reparative mandate of the ICC by funding services and activities that provide recognition, commemoration and material support through rehabilitative programmes.The TFV appeals to States Parties and other entities to contribute to the delivery of reparations to victims in urgent need, particularly in relation to the Ntaganda and Ongwen cases. The annual programme funding target of the TFV is set at a minimum of EUR 10 million.Contributions to the TFV qualify as Official Development Assistance (ODA)-eligible. TFV programmes for the benefit of victims of crimes under the jurisdiction of the ICC contribute to the broader impact of several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including peace, justice, and strong institutions (SDG 16), poverty reduction (SDG 1), good health and well-being (SDG 3), gender equality (SDG 5), decent work and economic growth (SDG 8), reduced inequalities (SDG 10), and climate action (SDG 13).For more information about the TFV, please contact trustfundforvictims@icc-cpi.int or visit www.trustfundforvictims.org. You can also follow TFV’s activities on X, LinkedIn, Bluesky, and Facebook.
