GC IV Commentary Series
articles.description: 2025 Commentary’s discussion of Common Article 2(2) - 2(3) has done a good job of clarifying these provisions, but more could have been done.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

Most discussion concerning Article 2 common (CA 2) to the four 1949 Geneva Conventions involves the first paragraph of the article, the application trigger for the law of armed conflict (LOAC) to “armed conflict which may arise between two or more of the High Contracting Parties,” or international armed conflict (IAC), as it has come to be known. However, the text of CA 2 also includes two additional, though much less frequently discussed paragraphs: a second paragraph addressing occupation; and a third paragraph discussing the application of LOAC to armed conflicts between States when not all belligerents are parties to the Conventions.
[(2)] The Convention shall also apply to all cases of partial or total occupation of the territory of a High Contracting Party, even if the said occupation meets with no armed resistance.

[(3)] Although one of the Powers in conflict may not be a party to the present Convention, the Powers who are parties thereto shall remain bound by it in their mutual relations. They shall furthermore be bound by the Convention in relation to the said Power, if the latter accepts and applies the provisions thereof.

A 2025 Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention (the Commentary ), by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), on paragraphs 2(2) and 2(3) is more extensive than a preceding 1958 Commentary (1956 in French) and is a very helpful addition to the corpus of discussion of these two paragraphs. However, the updated Commentary also raises three points worth closer examination: 1) belligerent occupation, including missed opportunities to clarify contemporary issues; 2) the requirement of an explicit statement for non-parties to not be bound by the Conventions; and 3) the potential application of the Conventions to “International Organizations” but not to non-States. This post addresses each of these three points in detail below.

Common Article 2 says very little about occupation, though the Fourth Geneva Convention (GC IV) offers quite a bit of detail in subsequent provisions with respect to laws that apply during occupation. It is important to note that CA 2(2) is not intended to refer to occupation generally, but only applies to the narrow situation of an unopposed occupation. As the 1958 Commentary makes clear,

The sense in which the paragraph under consideration should be understood is thus quite clear. It does not refer to cases in which territory is occupied during hostilities; in such cases the Convention will have been in force since the outbreak of hostilities or since the time war was declared. The paragraph only refers to cases where the occupation has taken place without a declaration of war and without hostilities, and makes provision for the entry into force of the Convention in those particular circumstances (p. 21).
articles.lede: 2025 Commentary’s discussion of Common Article 2(2) - 2(3) has done a good job of clarifying these provisions, but more could have been done.

articles.title: The President of the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute convened an event on International Criminal Justice, for the sake of future generations
articles.description: On 3 November 2026, the President of the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute, Ambassador Päivi Kaukoranta, convened an event entitled “International Criminal Justice: For the Sake of Future Generations”, at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, in cooperation with the Trust Fund for Victims.The event was honoured by the participation of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Mr Volker Türk, who provided the key note speech setting the context with his remarks focused on the lasting harms of crimes, the importance of intergenerational justice and of accountability as a measure of securing human rights in the future. As he remarked: “If accountability is to protect present and future generations, we must defend the institutions that make this possible (…). The ICC is an essential piece of the international human rights ecosystem, supported by the vast majority of United Nations Member States”. The address of the High Commissioner was followed by the remarks of Judge Rosario Salvatore Aitala, First Vice-President of the International Criminal Court and a panel event featuring Ms Nazhat Shameem Khan, Deputy Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court along with representatives of the victim communities and of the youth.; Mr Andres Parmas, President of the Board of Directors of the Trust Fund for Victims provided closing remarks. Participants in the event included States Parties, Court officials and civil society actors. The discussions, highlighted the importance of accountability, reparations, the preservation of memory and the prevention of future atrocities. Particular attention was devoted to the role of victims and young people in shaping the future of international justice, and to the contribution of reparative measures to restoring dignity, mitigating the long-term consequences of international crimes, promoting reconciliation and strengthening the foundations for lasting peace.The President of the Assembly of States Parties, Ambassador Päivi Kaukoranta, in commenting on the event, stated that: “International criminal justice is not only about addressing the gravest crimes committed in the past. It is also about shaping the future we wish to leave to generations to come : a future in which the rule of law prevails over impunity, accountability over indifference, and cooperation over division”.The Assembly of States Parties is the management oversight and legislative body of the ICC. It is comprised of representatives of States that have ratified and acceded to the Rome Statute. For additional information please contact the Assembly of States Parties via email at asp@icc-cpi.int.

Participants in the event included States Parties, Court officials and civil society actors. The discussions, highlighted the importance of accountability, reparations, the preservation of memory and the prevention of future atrocities. Particular attention was devoted to the role of victims and young people in shaping the future of international justice, and to the contribution of reparative measures to restoring dignity, mitigating the long-term consequences of international crimes, promoting reconciliation and strengthening the foundations for lasting peace.
The President of the Assembly of States Parties, Ambassador Päivi Kaukoranta, in commenting on the event, stated that:

“International criminal justice is not only about addressing the gravest crimes committed in the past. It is also about shaping the future we wish to leave to generations to come: a future in which the rule of law prevails over impunity, accountability over indifference, and cooperation over division”.
The Assembly of States Parties is the management oversight and legislative body of the ICC. It is comprised of representatives of States that have ratified and acceded to the Rome Statute.
For additional information please contact the Assembly of States Parties via email at asp@icc-cpi.int.

articles.title: The Swedish Commission closes the Nordic Sami reconciliation initiatives
articles.description: On September 30, 2026, Sweden has joined its Nordic neighbours in delivering a Sami Truth Commission report. Following five years of work and 270 interviews, its chair emphasised the urgent need for an official apology.
paragraphs: On September 30, 2026, the Truth Commission for the Sami People handed over its final report at its ceremonial closing in Staare/Östersund, Sweden. This was the last of the Nordic truth commissions for the Indigenous Sami people to conclude its work, following the Norwegian report delivered in 2023 and the Finnish report presented in 2025.

The ceremony was carried out in Swedish and some of the five different varieties of the Sami language, via an app’ for live interpretation. Several hundreds of people attended in person in the aula of the Staare/Östersund campus of the University of Mid-Sweden. Throughout the three hours of the ceremony, between 300 and 500 people watched the live broadcasting [still available online ]. The comment section proved a lively place for participants to express their own stories as well as support to others, either in Swedish, in Sami, or in emoji. Hearts and clapping hands flooded the comment section with each moving speech, flanked by messages expressing gratitude and personal experiences underscoring for example the need for language revitalization. It also came to function as a forum for translation questions, with attendees helping each other out. With the closing of the live stream, participants expressed hope and desire for implementation of the recommendations.

All the Nordic truth commissions have been influenced by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, which delivered its report in 2015. In his welcome speech at the handover ceremony, Jerker Bexelius, leader of the Gaaltije museum in Staare/Östersund, pointed out that it coincided with Canada’s national day for truth and reconciliation.

The commission, mandated by the Swedish government in 2021, began its work in June 2022, and has had three different chairs. At the ceremony, Lena Nyberg, who took over in April 2025, urged for an independent mechanism to monitor implementation of the truth commission’s calls to action and proposals. Furthermore, she called for increased autonomy of the Swedish Sami Parliament, a range of initiatives to increase the general public’s knowledge about Sami culture, history and rights, and measures to combat racism and discrimination against Sami. Nyberg also emphasised the need for an official apology — similar to the one already given by the Norwegian Parliament — and the urgent need for a special apology to elderly Sami who had been placed in so-called nomad schools or other boarding school facilities as children.

Different commissioners presented further findings and calls to action, highlighting the loss of language and culture, acts of resistance, the consequences of state and majority-population ignorance, and the Sami relationship to land use and ownership. These presentations were interspersed with readings of testimonies based on the personal narratives collected by the commission; circa 270 interviews as well as 40 written narratives and some focus group interviews with children and youth. Excerpts from these stories are presented in a separate part of the final report which was handed out to members of the audience.
articles.lede: On September 30, 2026, Sweden has joined its Nordic neighbours in delivering a Sami Truth Commission report. Following five years of work and 270 interviews, its chair emphasised the urgent need for an official apology.

The Law on Brain Technologies in Warfare Series – HUMINT, Detainees, and “Brain Fingerprinting”
cats: Law on Brain Technologies in Warfare Series
articles.description: The term “brain fingerprinting” may suggest a standard of reliability not matched by the result, as fingerprinting is more reliable.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: This post is an entry in our series on Air Commodore (ret.) William H. Boothby’s book, The Law on Brain Technologies in Warfare published by Elgar International.

As I outlined in a 2024 post, intelligence gathering has taken on an increasingly important role in the conduct of contemporary military operations. Its importance is reflected in Amy Zegart’s statement that “[i]n the twenty-first century, the tip of the spear isn’t a spear. It’s intelligence” ( Spies, Lies, and Algorithms, p. 43). Given the clandestine nature of many forms of intelligence gathering, it is perhaps fitting that the legal basis for such activity is almost innocuously tacked onto Article 24 of the 1907 Hague Land Warfare Regulations as “the employment of measures necessary for obtaining information about the enemy and the country are considered permissible.” Those measures include the collection of human intelligence (HUMINT), which is one of a wide range of intelligence categories that extends to categories such as SIGINT (signals intelligence), IMINT (image intelligence), MASINT (measurement and signature intelligence), GEOINT (geospatial intelligence), open-source intelligence (OSINT), CULTINT (cultural intelligence), and even CRIMINT (criminal intelligence).

HUMINT is often thought of primarily in terms of espionage involving human source contact operations. However, it more broadly includes screening the appearance, possessions, and attitudes of persons stopped at checkpoints during cordon and search, and with the handling of detainees, tactical questioning at the point of capture, and the exploitation of captured documents. It also involves: the debriefing of refugees, displaced persons, local civilians and your own forces; liaison operations with host and allied military and civilian authorities; and the interrogation of detainees (2006 Human Intelligence Collector Operations, paras. 1-4 to 1-27). Like many aspects of modern conflict, technological advances have had a significant impact on HUMINT operations. This is most directly through the use of social media to recruit and direct sources, and collect the intelligence they obtain (see here and here ).

As Bill Boothby identifies in his recent book, The Law on Brain Technologies in Warfare, there is also scope for using brain-related technology to monitor the thoughts of detained personnel while being interrogated for intelligence purposes. As he identifies, the current technology does not permit mind steering or mind reading. However, it might have a “utility in lie and deception detection and perhaps in revealing subconscious brain information (p. 279-80). The advantage of being able to confirm the veracity of what a detainee is saying is obvious. The scenario Boothby identifies (p. 280) is,

State A uses a BCI [Brain Computer Interface] system to obtain information from combatants from an enemy State B who have been captured during hostilities. The technique that is employed involves the wearing by a prisoner of an external headset. The prisoner is then asked a series of questions and their answers, together with the electrical brain activity as detected.
articles.lede: The term “brain fingerprinting” may suggest a standard of reliability not matched by the result, as fingerprinting is more reliable.

articles.title: 25th session of the ICC Assembly of States Parties, 30 November
articles.description: Share this page Twitter Twitter Twitter Mail ES
articles.lede: From 30 November to 7 December 2026, States Parties to the Rome Statute will gather in The Hague for the 25th session of the ICC Assembly of States Parties (ASP25).
paragraphs: From 30 November to 7 December 2026, States Parties to the Rome Statute will gather in The Hague for the 25th session of the ICC Assembly of States Parties (ASP25).

The Assembly is the management oversight and legislative body of the Court. Meeting in full plenary once a year, States Parties take decisions that are critical to the effective functioning of the Court and the broader Rome Statute system.

ASP25 takes place at a critical moment for international justice. As attacks against the ICC, its officials, civil society organisations and others supporting its mandate have intensified, the Assembly provides States Parties with an essential opportunity to demonstrate, through concrete action, their commitment to an independent and effective Court and to protect the integrity of the Rome Statute system.

Civil society will be present throughout the session, monitoring discussions, engaging with States Parties and Court officials, advocating for a fair, effective, and independent ICC, while ensuring that the perspectives of victims, survivors, and human rights defenders remain at the heart of deliberations on justice and accountability.

At its twenty-fifth session, the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute (ASP) will elect six judges to fill one-third of the International Criminal Court’s 18 judicial seats, following the regular three-year election cycle. The six newly elected judges will each serve for a nine-year term from 2027 to 2036.

Judicial elections are among the most significant governance functions of the Assembly. The quality, independence, and diversity of the Court’s bench directly shape the ICC’s credibility, jurisprudential development, and operational performance. The Rome Statute establishes a detailed legal framework designed to ensure that judges are selected based on merit, integrity, and representativeness, while subsequent Assembly resolutions have progressively strengthened transparency and due diligence safeguards.

Ahead of ASP25, civil society organisations and human rights defenders from every region share their priorities and recommendations for strengthening justice through the ICC and the Rome Statute system.

These contributions are more than statements: they reflect the lived realities of those on the frontlines of accountability efforts. Throughout ASP25, #NGOVoices will continue to spotlight these perspectives, ensuring that decisions taken in The Hague reflect the needs and insights of those working for justice around the world
In the margins of ASP25, civil society, States and the Court and other actors organise multiple side events.

Side events represent a unique opportunity to raise #NGOVoices around specific topics of mutual concern, including situations under investigation or preliminary examination, victims’ participation in confirmation of charges hearings, judicial and political developments related to the ICC and the ASP, threats and attacks against the international justice system, and other issues related to the ICC and the Rome Statute system.

The ICJ and Factual Controversy in Advisory Proceedings: Deference in Factual Determinations?
articles.description: ICJ's approach in 2025 Obligations of Israel advisory opinion raises important questions regarding the nature of the advisory function.
paragraphs: The advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) of 22 October 2025 concerning Obligations of Israel in relation to the Presence and Activities of the United Nations, Other International Organizations and Third States in and in relation to the Occupied Palestinian Territory ( Presence and Activities) addressed two main issues: Israel’s obligations relating to humanitarian relief in the West Bank; and (more significantly) Gaza, as well as Israel’s obligations in relation to the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA). Both these issues raised factual controversies, requiring the Court to make of its own factual determinations if it was to render an opinion on the pertinent issues.

Evidently, instead of exercising its discretion and declining to deliver an advisory opinion, in whole or in part, pursuant to Article 65 of its Statute, the Court did deliver an opinion, incidentally making factual determinations. Yet the Court’s approach in these and other proceedings raise important questions regarding the nature of the advisory function and perhaps whether the Court’s rhetoric on the nature of its advisory function withstands scrutiny when tested against its practice.

In this post, I shall first provide some background on the problem of factual uncertainty in the World Court’s advisory jurisprudence, before briefly recalling how the Court considered the controversial factual issues in its October 2025 opinion. I shall then consider the procedure through which the Court presented the evidence underlying its conclusions, while comparing this procedure to the one it would most likely have followed were the proceedings in question contentious. I shall conclude by offering some observations on how we should view the Court’s approach to questions of evidence, particularly in light of its prior jurisprudence on deference regarding factual questions. I should emphasise that the purpose of this post is not to consider the extent to which the Court’s factual assessments were correct but to focus simply on its approach to factual questions as such.

For over a century, the World Court has been faced with disputed questions of fact in advisory proceedings. In its 1923 (non-)advisory opinion on the Status of Eastern Carelia, after concluding that the Council of the League of Nations requested an advisory opinion ultra vires, the ICJ’s predecessor, the Permanent Court of International Justice (PCIJ), proceeded to provide “other cogent reasons which render it very inexpedient” to deliver an opinion. One such “cogent reason” was that there were factual issues of relevance for determining the status of Eastern Carelia which were strongly disputed by Finland and Russia. In this regard, the PCIJ noted that it

… does not say that there is an absolute rule that the request for an advisory opinion may not involve some enquiry as to facts, but, under ordinary circumstances, it is certainly expedient that the facts upon which the opinion of the Court is desired should not be in controversy, and it should not be left to the Court itself to ascertain what they are.
articles.lede: ICJ's approach in 2025 Obligations of Israel advisory opinion raises important questions regarding the nature of the advisory function.

articles.title: ICC President addresses United Nations General Assembly, Calls for renewed support amid threats
articles.description: The President of the International Criminal Court (ICC), Judge Tomoko Akane, today addressed the United Nations General Assembly to present the Court's annual report, outlining key judicial developments, reparations activities, cooperation efforts, and the challenges facing the institution. For the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, the President addressed General Assembly by way of a pre-recorded video, following the United States' imposition of sanctions against the Court on 9 October 2026.In her address, President Akane reaffirmed the Court's determination to fulfil its judicial mandate despite sanctions, threats and other challenges facing the institution. "Despite all the challenges, the International Criminal Court will continue to carry out its judicial mandate with full independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence. In so doing, the Court is firmly resolved to contribute to the rule of law in the international community".In relation to the Court's judicial activities, President Akane noted that proceedings continued to advance at every stage, from investigations and arrest warrants to confirmation of charges, trials, appeals and reparations. Victims remained at the centre of the Court's work. During the reporting period, more than 23,500 victims participated in proceedings before the Court, including more than 7,000 at the reparations stage. The President highlighted the central importance of cooperation in the execution of arrest warrants. At present, 34 publicly known arrest warrants remained outstanding. "For States Parties, cooperation is a legal obligation under Part 9 of the Statute, and the obligation to arrest and surrender lies at its heart", she said.President Akane also emphasised that broader participation in the Rome Statute system remains essential to strengthening the Court's legitimacy. She welcomed Hungary's decision to revoke its notification of withdrawal, while noting that six States notified their withdrawal during the reporting period.The President expressed appreciation for the cooperation and support provided by the United Nations. “The United Nations is a key partner of the Court. In line with the 2004 Relationship Agreement, the Court continued to receive crucial support from United Nations entities, departments, offices and special advisers and representatives of the Secretary-General, including in the field, where the United Nations directly supported 61 missions”, she stated. Concluding her remarks, President Akane called on States and the international community to continue supporting the institution created under the Rome Statute to combat impunity for the world's gravest crimes. "History will judge how the international community protected the Court and the mandate entrusted to it by the Rome Statute. The time to act is now", she stated.ICC President Speech to the United Nations General Assembly, 02.11.2026Annual report of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations General AssemblyFor more information, please contact the ICC Public Affairs Unit: PublicAffairs.Unit@icc-cpi.int. articles.title: Cases against Italy before European Court of Human Rights could clarify States’ duty to cooperate with international justice amid mounting threats to the ICC
articles.description: Italy's ICC cooperation is challenged before the European Court of Human Rights as NGOs intervene in cases concerning the release of a Libya war crimes suspect.
paragraphs: 2 November 2026 – REDRESS, Route Justice, TRIAL International, and the International Federation for Human Rights ( FIDH) have submitted third-party interventions to the European Court of Human Rights in two cases challenging Italy’s failure to surrender Osama Elmasry Njeem to the International Criminal Court (ICC). While REDRESS, Route Justice, and TRIAL international argue that States’ human rights obligations generally require them to cooperate with the ICC to ensure accountability for torture and other international crimes, FIDH’s intervention addresses the admissibility of the applications

The cases ( Y v. Italy and Z v. Italy) concern Osama Elmasry Njeem, who was wanted by the ICC for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Libya. He was arrested in Italy in January 2025, released two days later and returned to Libya on a State flight.

These cases raise a question with implications far beyond Italy: when surrendering a suspect to an international court is essential to securing accountability, can a State’s failure to cooperate breach its human rights obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights?
The victims in the case allege that Italy’s conduct breached its obligations under the rights to life and freedom from torture.

REDRESS, Route Justice, and TRIAL International argue that a suspect’s presence on a State’s territory, a request for arrest and surrender from a competent international court, international obligations to investigate the alleged crimes, and the absence of a realistic alternative avenue for accountability can together establish the jurisdictional link needed to engage the State’s procedural obligations under Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention (the right to life and the prohibition of torture). Once those obligations are engaged, they may require meaningful cooperation with the international court where this is reasonably necessary to secure effective accountability.

The intervention asks the European Court to recognise that, where international proceedings offer the only realistic prospect of accountability, States must use the powers reasonably available to them diligently, effectively, and in good faith. Their conduct must be assessed against their wider international obligations, including obligations under the Rome Statute and the peremptory prohibitions of torture and crimes against humanity.

FIDH has filed a separate third-party intervention in the same cases. It argues that the Assembly of States Parties’ non-cooperation procedure following an ICC finding does not bar individual applications under the European Convention. FIDH maintains that the procedures concern different parties and complaints, and that the Assembly’s procedure is not comparable to an international investigation or settlement, given its distinct features and potential effects, which differ from those of individual applications seeking redress for violations of Convention rights.

The cases come at a critical moment for the ICC, which faces sanctions and other measures aimed at obstructing its work and intimidating those who work for or cooperate with it. These threats make effective State cooperation all the more important to safeguarding access to international justice.
articles.lede: Italy's ICC cooperation is challenged before the European Court of Human Rights as NGOs intervene in cases concerning the release of a Libya war crimes suspect.

paragraphs: Held from 19 to 21 May 2026, the confirmation of charges hearing against Khaled Mohammed Ali El Hishri in the Libya situation marked an important procedural milestone before the International Criminal Court (ICC), as the first case resulting from the ICC’s 15-year investigation into Libya to reach this phase. Following the hearing, on 16 July 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber I unanimously confirmed all 17 charges against El Hishri and committed the case to trial.

In this context, the Victims’ Rights Working Group (VRWG), with Libya Crimes Watch, Lawyers for Justice in Libya (a working name of Route Justice), Refugees in Libya and the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR) have prepared this briefing note to contribute to more accessible and inclusive proceedings at the ICC, and ensure they are responsive to the experiences and needs of victims.

The recommendations draw on direct observations during the El Hishri confirmation of charges hearing, consultations with victims and survivors present at or otherwise engaged in the hearing, and exchanges with Libyan and international CSOs before, during and after the proceedings. The briefing focuses on the experience of affected communities engaging with and attending proceedings at the seat of the Court. The recommendations do not seek to assess the merits of the criminal case, but to identify practical measures through which future ICC proceedings can become safer, more accessible and more responsive to victims and survivors.

The VRWG is a network of 181 civil society organisations working to uphold the rights and interests of victims in International Criminal Court (ICC) proceedings. Co-led by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), REDRESS and the Coalition for the ICC, the VRWG was reconvened in 2024 to renew its engagement on victims’ rights at the ICC, including contributing to the Court’s review of its 2012 Victims’ Strategy.

articles.title: “Trump has succeeded through the law”
articles.description: Ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on November 3, 2026—with the American president struggling to retain majority in Congress —Samuel Moyn, professor of law and history at Yale University, examines the record of the second Trump presidency and its approach to international justice.
paragraphs: SAMUEL MOYN: Donald Trump’s first term is very different from his second term. I think he was feared to be an authoritarian or a despot from before he was elected in 2016. But in his first term, he proved blocked, probably as much by the Republican party as by his own servants. And he was also very disorganized: it wasn’t clear what he was trying to achieve, he didn’t do a lot. When it comes to something I’m very concerned about, which is America’s international war making, he probably did fewer illegal things. His first term involved less death of Americans and non-Americans through war than his predecessors.

Now his second term is very distinctive because its first year showed that he had learned from his mistakes the first time. He came into office with more loyal servants, and they had made a plan that he implemented. Both terms have been characterised by a lesson for all of us in the fact that the law is made to be interpreted and Donald Trump has succeeded through the law, not mainly through breaking the law.
“In the second term, mostly the Supreme Court has been on Trump’s side. It hasn’t required him to break the law, because he was allowed to remake the law.”

The Supreme Court has allowed much of his agenda in both terms. The most obvious example in the first term would be the travel ban [for nationals from Iran, Syria, Sudan, Libya, Somalia, and Yemen] which the Supreme Court permitted. In the second term, mostly the Supreme Court has been on Trump’s side. It hasn’t required him to break the law, because he was allowed to remake the law.

Yes, there were multiple illegal acts in the boat strikes in the Caribbean. But in the end, these were kind of relatively minor in the scheme of American imperial history in this hemisphere and since World War II around the world. Those are troubling, but the decapitation of the Venezuelan regime, its true significance is that it was a stepping stone that allowed him to feel very overconfident about the attack on Iran.

It was, I would say, flagrantly illegal. Under international law, that could be debated. But it was in the nature of a deal with Maduro’s henchmen and women who were happy to take his place. It showed that Trump doesn’t care about the law. He’s willing to be very reckless, but he also understood what the American people would support. The Maduro strike probably wasn’t that unpopular, and its consequences were slight from the American point of view, whereas the Iran war has been disastrous.

“What has changed, I think, is not a pattern of illegality which has been endemic for decades. But once again, we have a president who promised to be a peace president and does something extremely unpopular with the American people, the Iran war.”

What has changed, I think, is not a pattern of illegality which has been endemic for decades. But once again, we have a president who promised to be a peace president and does something extremely unpopular with the American people, the Iran war.

With every new case, the president’s lawyers will say that it’s another legal step, and his critics will say it’s something that has never been done before. And of course, every act is distinctive and new in some way. But if we’re honest, we have had American hemispheric regime change over and over. Basically, since the late 19th century, it’s almost a regular occurrence.
